GAMINGGUIDE
Elden Ring: 10 Best Dexterity Weapons You Shouldn’t Sleep On



Behold the best dexterity weapons in all of the Lands Between 

Whether you’re an Astrologer or a Vagabond, Elden Ring‘s huge arsenal of weapons always has something available for every build you can think of. But if you’ve played the game for a while, you’d know that the weapons which scale with dexterity often take home the prize for being tremendously overpowered.

You’ll find a plethora of these awesome instruments of destruction in the game, so much in fact that it might become hard to figure out which ones are actually useful. So to cut you some slack, let’s take a look at only the top 10 best dexterity weapons in Elden Ring that you just can’t sit out on.

(1/10)

Hand of Malenia
Hand of Malenia
Wielding Requirements: Str 16, Dex 48

Scaling: Str E, Dex C

Highlights: You can use the Waterfowl Dance; there’s no need for anything else

- Advertisement -

After reaching the Haligtree and beating Malenia, you’ll be rewarded with her Remembrance which you can exchange with Enia for the Hand of Malenia, a katana built in the image of Malenia’s prosthetic arm. The Hand of Malenia is similar to the other katanas in Elden Ring in the sense that it possesses Bleed damage, but where it outshines them is with its longer size — yay, more hitboxes.

Getting the Hand of Malenia is by no means easy, but manage to do that, and you’ll be just as invincible as the Rot Goddess herself. The dexterity scaling on it is nothing short of amazing too, and if you’re rocking two of these bad boys in New Game+, then it’ll be game over for the bosses. And before I forget, yes, equipping the Hand allows you to use the most unfair and broken move in the history of video games, the Waterfowl Dance.

(2/10)

Moonveil
Moonveil
Wielding Requirements: Str 12, Dex 18, Int 23

Scaling: Str E, Dex D, Int C

- Advertisement -

Highlights: Magic damage

Unsurprisingly, my next pick for the best dexterity weapons in Elden Ring list happens to be another katana, the Moonveil. It has got a mix of dexterity, Intelligence, and strength scaling, so it’s a great all-rounder in terms of power.

Thanks to its Intelligence scaling, every slice of the Moonveil has a splash of magic damage infused in it, and when the slashes feel too repetitive, its dual special move mode allows you to cut up foes in all sorts of pieces. On the other hand, there’s the Rivers of Blood as well, a neat alternative to the Moonveil. They’re basically the same thing, but while the Moonveil is unmatched in dexterity, the Rivers of Blood is an overall powerhouse. You can read more about it in this listicle of best Elden Ring weapons.

(3/10)

Godskin Peeler
Godskin Peeler
- Advertisement -

Wielding Requirements: Str 17, Dex 22

Scaling: Str E, Dex C

Highlights: Rapid flurry of attacks

The Godskin Peeler is the most menacing Twinblade you’ll come across in Elden Ring. One end of this terrifying pole is a needle for shanking enemies, while the other takes the form of a sickle for causing excruciating pain. Combining both sides, you get to unleash spinning slashes in quick succession onto your enemies.

Unfortunately, the Peeler doesn’t come included with Bleed, but what it lacks in passives it makes up for with its Black Flame Tornado ability that you can spam endlessly. So yeah, it’s among the best dexterity weapons Elden Ring has to offer.

(4/10)

Bolt of Gransax
Bolt of Gransax
Wielding Requirements: Str 20, Dex 40

Scaling: Str D, Dex D

Highlights: Lightning damage, Pretty much a sniper rifle

There aren’t many dexterity weapons in Elden Ring that come infused with Lightning damage, but from those that do have that wonderful little bonus, the Bolt of Gransax stands out clearly. It’s a spear that scales brilliantly with a strength-dexterity build, and besides obliterating foes in front of you, it’s also a really deadly sniper rifle because of its special ability.

Its Ancient Lightning Spear skill causes your character to jump in the air and summon a lightning bolt which is then thrown at enemies. The range is unbelievably far, plus, the Bolt of Gransax does 20% additional damage against those pesky dragons, so if close combat isn’t your thing, you know what to do. 

(5/10)

Bloodhound Claws
Bloodhound claws
Wielding Requirements: Str 10, Dex 15

Scaling: Str D, Dex D

Highlights: Bleed damage, Scales equally well with both strength & dexterity

You’ve got to admit at some point in your life you’ve imagined yourself playing hero with Wolverine’s Adamantium claws. Well, you can thank Miyazaki sensei as the vicious Bloodhound Claws do the perfect job of replicating that sensation.

The Bloodhound’s Claws rip and tear through the toughest of bosses, albeit you will have to get closer to enemies than you’d like. And last but not least, the Bloodhound Claws come preloaded with the broken Bloodhound’s Step Ash of War, so landing those backstabs couldn’t be any easier — or if you just want the Bloodhound’s Step, here’s a guide on finding it.

(6/10)

Golden Order Greatsword
Golder Order Greatsword
Wielding Requirements: Str 16, Dex 21, Fai 28

Scaling: Str E, Dex D, Fai C

Highlights: Scales well with both dexterity and faith

The Golden Order Greatsword primarily scales with faith, but don’t you always need to have a little faith in your weapons am I right? The dexterity scaling on it isn’t too bad either, so if you’re going for an incantation build, using this chunky golden Greatsword as your main melee armament wouldn’t be a bad idea.

You can obtain the Golden Order Greatsword by defeating the Misbegotten Crusader found in the Cave of the Forlorn in the Consecrated Snowfield. It’s a tough sword to get, but like all the best dexterity weapons in Elden Ring, once it’s in your hands, no one’s safe from certain death.

(7/10)

Bloodhound’s Fang
Bloodhound fang
Wielding Requirements: Str 18, Dex 17

Scaling: Str D, Dex C

Highlights: Earliest weapon you can find with the Bloodhound’s Step, Bleed damage

This Bleed weapon is basically a game-changer, and if you’re new to Elden Ring and curious about the strange “Bloodhound’s Step” passive ability the community keeps yapping on about, then you should set your sights on the Bloodhound’s Fang. The Bloodhound’s Fang will likely be the first Bleed imbued weapon you’ll come across in Elden Ring, and aside from being a good fit with a dexterity character, it’s got a nice moveset of combos to cut up enemies.

This Curved Greatsword is an obvious choice to recommend to new players who aren’t good with Soulslikes. Apart from the deadly slashes and lots of Bleed, the nice little cherry on top is that it comes with the Bloodhound’s Step ability that allows you to dodge just about any attack thrown at you. Seriously, if easy mode was an option, this would be it.

(8/10)

Wing of Astel
Wing of astel
Wielding Requirements: Str 7, Dex 17, Int 20

Scaling: Str E, Dex D, Int D

Highlights: Magic damage, Handy skill

You’ll find the Wing of Astel pretty late-game, but even so, it’s a terrific weapon if your character specializes in sorcery and dexterity. The light and heavy attacks with the Wing of Astel are the usual swings you’d expect from a Curved Greatsword, but its skill is as devastating as it is stylish.

With the Nebula ability, you can either summon a dark cloud that will scatter explosive magic stars in an area in front of you or perform a sweep attack that also ends with a bang, albeit a smaller one. The killer sword strikes aside, the Wing of Astel has got some of the best spells in Elden Ring attached to it.

(9/10)

Vyke’s War Spear
Greatspear
Wielding Requirements: Str 16, Dex 20, Fai 18

Scaling: Str E, Dex C, Fai D

Highlights: Inflicts Madness 

After playing around with Vyke’s War Spear for dozens of hours, I can confirm you’ll go mad — literally. It does a ton of damage, has great reach, an awesome special ability, and scales masterfully with hybrid dexterity builds, but it comes with a major drawback: its Ash of War applies madness to both the enemy and wielder.

Because of the tricky repercussions of using Vyke’s War Spear, it’s not something you should use recklessly. Try to find that sweet spot of choosing the right chain of attacks, and once you nail that down, the War Spear becomes a joy to impale mobs with.

(10/10)

Eleonora’s Poleblade
Eleonora Poleblade
Wielding Requirements: Str 12, Dex 21, Arc 19

Scaling: Str E, Dex D, Arc D

Highlights: Arcane scaling, Causes blood loss build-up 

Unlike the Godskin Peeler, Eleonora’s Poleblade does not have a spectacular reach, but it wouldn’t hurt to overlook that in exchange for some fire damage and blood loss build-up. Eleonora’s Poleblade comes with another perk as well: it scales with arcane and dexterity. Arcane scaling isn’t something many weapons in Elden Ring have, so for builds relying heavily on Dragon Breath Incantations, Eleonora’s Poleblade is a must-have.

Despite the short-handedness, you’ll be swirling around the entire battlefield cutting foes up through the courtesy of the Bloodblade Dance skill. Triggering the skill has you leap up into the air and then reign in on those below with a rapid shower of strikes. The Bloodblade Dance is perhaps the most offensive skill in the entire game, so if for nothing else, consider using Eleonora’s Poleblade for the arcane and lethal special technique.

But even if they aren’t looking to flip veterans at the deadline any more, finding players who are under-priced by the market is still an important tactic for teams to pursue in a league with a hard salary cap like the NHL has. In a sense, the NHL has become an efficiency competition, so adding players who provide value on-ice above what they’re being paid is wise for contenders and rebuilding teams alike.

The Leafs have a bit of a logjam at forward right now, with eight veterans under contract for next season and a large group of prospects who will be fighting for ice time. Q:

Why can't the compiler find this operator<< overload?

I'm trying to write overloads of operator<< for specific instantiations of standard library containers that will be stored in a boost::variant. Here's a small example that illustrates the problem:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

std::ostream & operator<<( std::ostream & os, const std::vector< int > & ) {
  os << "Streaming out std::vector< int >";
  return os;
}

std::ostream & operator<<( std::ostream & os, const std::vector< double > & ) {
  os << "Streaming out std::vector< double >";
  return os;
}

#include <boost/variant.hpp>

typedef boost::variant< std::vector< int >, std::vector< double > > MyVariant;

int main( int argc, char * argv[] ) {
  std::cout << MyVariant();
  return 0;
}

Clang's first error is
boost/variant/detail/variant_io.hpp:64:14: error: invalid operands to binary expression ('std::basic_ostream<char>' and 'const std::vector<int, std::allocator<int>>')
        out_ << operand;
        ~~~~ ^  ~~~~~~~

I realize that the #include <boost/variant.hpp> is in an odd place. I'm pretty sure the problem had to do with two-phase name lookup in templates, so I moved the #include in an attempt to implement fix #1 from the clang documentation on lookup. Fix #2 from that documentation isn't a good option because I believe adding my overloaded operator<< to the std namespace would lead to undefined behavior.
Shouldn't defining my operator<<s before the #include allow the compiler to find the definitions? That technique seems to work in the following example, adapted from the same clang page.
#include <iostream>

namespace ns {
  struct Data {};
}

std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& out, const ns::Data & data) {
  return out << "Some data";
}

namespace ns2 {
  template<typename T>
  void Dump( std::ostream & out, const T & value) {
    out << value;
  }
}

int main( int argc, char * argv[] ) {
  ns2::Dump( std::cout, ns::Data() );
}

A:

During template instantiation function template depending on a template type are only found during phase II look-up. Phase II look-up doesn't consider names visible at the point of use but only considers names found based on argument dependent look-up. Since the only associated namespace for std::ostream and std::vector<int> is namespace std it doesn't look for your output operators defined in the global namespace. Of course, you are not allowed to add these operators to namespace std which is a real catch: you can only define these operators for containers involving, at least, one user define type! On possibly way around this restriction is to add a custom allocator which is simply derived from std::allocator<T> but lives in a suitable user-define namespace: you can then define the output operators in this namespace. The drawback of this approach is that std::vector<T> (i.e., without an allocator parameter) is pretty much a vocabulary type.
Moving the declarations around doesn't help: phase II name look-up doesn't really depend on the order of the declaration except that the declarations have to precede the point of instantiation. The only proper fix is to define the operators in a namespace being sought by phase II look-up which pretty much means that the types being printed have to involve a user-defined type.

I opened my eyes, seeing only a black void around me. I felt as if there was no ground below me, no air going through my nostrils. "Ah... I'm dreaming." Out of the corner of my eye, I saw a flash of light and from it emerged a blue sphere with a white circle engraved on it, making it similar to an eye. A female voice echoed, repeating "The Blue Pillar will change a nation's fate. The Black Pillar cracks under a war's weight. The White Pillar is hidden behind veils. The Green Pillar's protection fails. The Red Pillar guards an empty throne filled with hate." Was it a prophetic dream or was I thinking too much about the war in my own nation? Most dreams are often works of our own minds. I simply waited for the dream to end. Upon opening my eyes, the first thing I saw was a pair of golden eyes peering at me. I stiffened and quickly sat up. "Kunnebudo, you scared me!" She giggled and began to speak in Hazrunic. "Oh, the area translator was returned to the guards." I said, pointing to the entrance. Hearing my incomprehensible words, Kunnebudo seemed to wilt. The device was so useful that I told myself I'd save some money to buy one of my own. I looked around and saw our companions getting ready for the day.
A variety of small recipients was scattered on the ground and from them the Hazrun dipped their fingers and painted themselves with ink. Manmurekan used red to paint around her eyes, Kuşien used yellow to draw the vertical lines under her eyes, and Taokar used various colours to paint his arms and chest. Kunnebudo signalled for me to help paint her back, moving her index finger in an imaginary drawing for me to replicate. I was unfamiliar with this custom. The bodypaint appeared to be symbolic of attributes each of them wished to represent or reinforce, so what could back painting mean? Kunnebudo lifted up her tunic, showing me her smooth-skinned grey back. I took some yellow dye and did my best to replicate the design she showed me. When I finished, she showed it to Taokar, who nodded in approval. Kunnebudo dipped her finger in green and drew something on my throat. Perhaps its purpose was to help me communicate with them.
After a quick breakfast and final checks on our gear, we prepared to leave. I approached the guards one more time, requesting to borrow the area translator so we could finalise our plans. With the device once again allowing us to communicate, Manmurekan took out a map, comparing it against the one etched into the outpost’s stone wall. “Look,” she said, pointing out the inconsistencies between them. Some paths shown on the wall didn’t appear on our map, and vice versa. “There might be shrines or old outposts not listed here,” Manmurekan mused, her finger tracing potential routes. “We should consider hunting along the way,” I suggested. “Not only for food but maybe we can trade at the next village.” The group agreed. Our journey took a new turn with this plan. We would make for the village near the next outpost, aiming to resupply, possibly finding work, given our dwindling funds. Taokar, with his boisterous confidence, declared, “Nothing like a good hunt to start the day!”
We managed to hunt successfully, and by the time we reached the village, we were laden with more than just food. There were herbs and other miscellanea we had collected along the way, hopeful they might fetch a price. In the heart of the village, without the translator, our interactions became a mix of gestures, smiles, and the few words of the languages I knew. I offered healing where I could, and the villagers’ initial wariness gave way to gratitude. Coins, food, and even a few trinkets were gifted in return. It was then we heard of a creature troubling the village’s outskirts. A concerned human villager told us through Kuşien's translations, the concern evident in his eyes. It had attacked their goats, but they were apprehensive about the thing developing a taste for people.
My companions and I exchanged looks. This could be the work we were looking for. Not what I had expected, but perhaps what we needed. Tasks in the villages often involved mending fences and the sort, not facing beasts, yet the decision was unanimous without a word spoken. I found myself agreeing to hunt the unknown animal, or at least to heal those who were going to hunt it. The villager produced a crude drawing on paper of a quadrupedal creature with two blank circles for eyes. It prepared to attack a goat under the moonlight, a crescent and stars adorning the sky. With this it was evident that it appeared at night. We planned to wait for night to fall, hide where the goats were gathered, and ambush the creature when it attacked. Until then, it sounded like a good idea to just relax on the village. The alpine scenery was different from the pine-covered forests of my home village.
Our afternoon venture into the village, with the group occasionally splitting to explore, found Kunnebudo and me paired by an unspoken agreement. Taokar, eager to earn more coins, went to help the inn's owner with carrying and chopping a great amount of wood. Kuşien disappeared to some unknown corner of the village (or even outside of it) and Manmurekan  volunteered to care for our belongings on that same inn. The group had agreed to meet up there at twilight. Without the aid of the area translator, my interaction with Kunnebudo was a series of comedic misinterpretations, her attempts at conveying thoughts often leading to humorous confusion. Kunnebudo seemed to find the village fascinating. She wandered with wide eyes and, drawing chuckles from vendors as she examined their wares with exaggerated wonder, once holding up a simple spoon as if it were a relic.
As the evening approached, we regrouped at the village inn for our meal. The villagers inside cast sidelong glances in our direction, their curiosity piqued yet veiled by a layer of apprehension. Seated at an isolated table, our presence remained a silent island amidst the murmurs. The gap in language and familiarity lingered. Dinner was served in generous portions, probably in gratitude to Taokar’s help earlier. As we ate, the initial reservations of the village folk seemed to soften, curiosity slowly overtaking their wariness. In a moment inspired perhaps by the easing atmosphere, Kuşien retrieved her flute. The first notes grew into a soothing melody. The music enveloped villagers and travellers alike. The performance was met with applause from the gathered patrons, their earlier reservations seemingly washed away by music. Taokar, seizing the moment, engaged the closer villagers with a blend of charades and laughter, his demeanour disarmingly genuine.
The innkeeper, now openly warm, brought forward rounds of a locally brewed drink, a gesture of communal hospitality. “To new friends!” he proclaimed. Other patrons took their own instruments and began playing with Kuşien. The songs were strange at first, since the Hazrun musical tradition is very different from those of the other races, but they adapted and played a beautiful blend of Sulcai, human, and Hazrun music. When they finished, Kuşien bowed to the audience, even if a bit awkwardly, and returned to her seat among us. She was trying to suppress a smile and it felt good to finally see her free from her worries and painful memories. Taokar then began an arm-wrestling competition and I could see the difference of strength that his race had. I glanced at Kunnebudo’s hands, who was making imaginary shapes on the table, and saw that her knuckles were hardened and calloused, probably from punching. Was she a martial artist?
We left in good spirits, though I noticed Kuşien's gloom had returned. Or was it focus? We were going to hunt a potentially dangerous creature so it was understandable. It would have been ideal for the moon to be full. It was instead waxing, which made visibility lower. The group divided in a formation designed to attack the creature from any direction. To the north and south, Kuşien and Manmurekan respectively, since they could both attack at a distance. To the west was Taokar and to the east, me and Kunnebudo. Through a punching and kicking performance earlier, they showed be Kunnebudo was indeed a martial artist. Since she was unarmed and was less resistant than Taokar, I would provide her assistance and healing.
I don't know how much time passed until a humanoid silhouette crawled into view. It appeared from among the trees, its gait cautious and unnerving. It was as if the thing was not a wild animal, but something else that possessed intelligence. It looked around and appeared to sniff the air the way its head bobbed. It slowly turned its head in my direction despite being dozens of paces away. Had it noticed me? I was sure I was well hidden. I looked at Kunnebudo, who was looking fixedly at our target, her lips parted without uttering a word. I turned to look at it again and it was gone. "South." She murmured. "Manmurekan tsu yonpe." While I struggled to translate the words other than south and our companion's name, Kunnebudo darted at an incredible speed southwards. As she sprinted through the grass, I scrambled to keep up. Up ahead, the faint glow of Manmurekan’s fire magic flickered like a beacon.
The creature, its form grotesquely humanoid, moved with an eerie intention that sent shivers down my spine. It advanced towards Manmurekan, who stood firm and ready, her flames crackling in her hands. Kuşien’s arrows whistled through the dark from the north. However, they found no mark. The creature’s agility was disconcerting. As Taokar approached from the west, his axe raised high, the creature shifted with a swift, mocking grace. When Kunnebudo and I finally reached Manmurekan’s side, the latter had already engaged. The creature lunged at her, slashing with its twisted claws. Manmurekan dodged a swipe, but not quickly enough. A second strike caught her across the shoulder, drawing four red lines across her porcelain-white skin. She winced but kept her stance, retaliating with a burst of flame. With the flash of light from her spell, I could now see the creature. Its discoloured, greyish-white skin revealed a myriad of dark veins and prominent bones underneath it. The limbs were long and gangly, even if they appeared to hold some strength, and ended in twisted fingers armed with claws. Its scalp had vestiges of white hair, its face eerily human-like, though lacking ears and nose. Its large round eyes had no pupils and seemed to emit a faint glow, while the mouth, too wide for the slightly elongated face, was unnervingly devoid of teeth.
Seeing Manmurekan wounded, I scrambled to her side. My hands glowed with a healing light, reaching out to touch the wounded area. The light enveloped her shoulder, and she gritted her teeth, a mix of pain and relief flashing across her face as the wound began to close. “Good,” she grunted, not sparing a glance at her healing flesh, her attention unwavering from the creature. “Remain close. Heal, no fight.” Kunnebudo danced around the creature, her strikes a series of rapid, precise blows that seemed to startle it. This distraction allowed Manmurekan to prepare another spell, her hands weaving hand seals and her fingers sparking with gathering energy. Suddenly, the creature turned its soulless gaze towards me. A cold dread filled me. I had only my healing, no offensive magic. I stepped back, tripping over a rock. I was no warrior, and the line between duty and survival blurred as the thing leapt at me. A well-placed arrow hit one of its eyes, spouting a foul-smelling dark ichor and sending the creature tumbling to the side. I could see Taokar still closing the distance between us, so it was up to either Kunnebudo or Manmurekan to finish it. The creature raised itself with its gaunt limbs, the arrow still in its eye socket. Kunnebudo delivered a strong kick on its elbow, the cracking of the bone echoing through the night. With a broken limb and one less eye, it would surely be easier to end this thing. It sumbled about as a few more arrows hit its back. Manmurekan's spell had finally charged and a lightning bolt came from her hands, electrocuting the creature. A stench of burning flesh rose as it laid on the ground, its skin darkened from the thunder magic.
The tension within the group palpably decreased. The night was quiet again, save for a faint sizzling noise coming from the smoldering form on the ground. Kuşien approached cautiously, her bow lowered, her steps tentative as if expecting the creature to rise once more. Taokar finally reached our side, his heavy breaths echoing in the stillness. He asked a question, to which Kuşien responded with "Ayi", meaning "yes" in Hazrunic, her voice carrying a harsh weariness. She surveyed the corpse with a critical eye. I felt an uneasy churn in my stomach as I looked at the creature. It’s human-like features distorted in death were unsettling. Kunnebudo placed a comforting hand on my shoulder, her own expression unreadable in the dim light. Some villagers, awakened by the commotion, emerged from their homes, lanterns and torches in hand, illuminating the scene. Their faces bore a mix of fear, relief, and curiosity. One of the village elders, an old man with a silver beard and wise eyes, approached us. His gaze fell on the creature, and his relief was palpable.
"Good", "Work", "Gratitude", and "Fear" were the words I could comprehend from Kuşien’s translation from Sendralese to Hazrunic. Gratitude was offered in the form of enough food and supplies for at least five days. Taokar eagerly tried to organise a celebration right there, but the elder insisted on a proper feast at daybreak. Our group agreed, both out of respect and fatigue from the night’s ordeal. As we walked back to the inn, the reality of what had occurred settled in. We had faced danger together and were victorious. This was not something I had expected when I had first joined with the Hazrun. That night, surrounded by the soft snores of my companions, I felt as if I was truly part of the group, even with the racial and linguistic barrier. 
As the sun rose, we gathered with the villagers in a humble but spirited celebration. The food was plentiful, the music vibrant, and the atmosphere filled with a genuine camaraderie.
Villagers, once wary, now shared tables laden with local delicacies. The loud laughter of Taokar mingled with lutes and drums and the presence of a single area translator enabled us all to communicate (even if its effect affected a radius of only six paces). Kunnebudo led me through a dance, her movements as fluid as a winding river. Amid the noise of celebration, my attention was repeatedly drawn to Kuşien. Initially, she seemed enthralled, taking a break from her flute to appreciate the food and song of the different races of the Archbishopric united by the faith in Ma'at. However, as she noticed me laughing heartily with Kunnebudo and Taokar, her smile wavered and eventually broke. Silently, she slipped away from the gathering, her figure receding into the shadows at the edge of the village. Feeling concerned, I took the area translator by Manmurekan’s suggestion, then excused myself and followed the path Kuşien had taken, tracking her to the outskirts, where I found her perched on a fallen log, alone.
Approaching quietly, I overheard her murmuring to herself in Hazrunic, the lilting cadences of her speech marked by sighs of resignation. Though her words were incomprehensible due to the language barrier, their emotional weight was unmistakable. Taking a breath, I stepped forward, clearing my throat softly to announce my presence. Kuşien startled slightly, glancing up with welled-up eyes. Turning back to the underbrush, she plucked idly at the leaves, avoiding my gaze. “Sorry…” I started in her own language to hide the fact that I carried the area translator with me. She shook her head, emitting a brittle, dismissive laugh. “It’s nothing, Human,” she responded. “Just old memories stirred by...” She found herself unable to finish, her gaze settling on the ground. Sitting beside her on the log, I respected the space between us. She sighed, her eyes empty. “Seeing you there, laughing, sharing moments… it reminds me too much of him. You have his way, sometimes… it’s too much. Then it comes to my mind that he's not here anymore. But you are. And how can I have any peace of mind when Hadrian’s spitting image is travelling with me?”
Unseen by her, I pulled out the area translator I had kept hidden until that moment, unsure of whether I would need it. Now, as I discreetly fidgeted with it, her surprise was palpable when she finally noticed the artifact and I finally responded. “Kuşien, I understood everything you said.” I said softly, watching as a mix of shock, vulnerability, and finally, a reluctant relief crossed her features. “You should have told me.” She replied, her eyebrows furrowed. “I kept quiet because I thought you needed to speak freely, to vent a bit.” I explained. She tried to maintain eye contact but averted her eyes repeatedly. Kuşien nodded slowly, her demeanour still cautious, yet noticeably softening. “Thank you, Caelan,” she murmured, her previous coldness thawing slightly. “For listening.” We sat together for a while longer, the forest quiet around us. As we made our way back, approaching the edge of the festivities, Taokar caught sight of us returning together. His face split into a grin, and he couldn’t help but throw a teasing jab our way.
“And what were you two doing, sneaking off like that?” he bellowed, laughter rumbling in his throat. His question, meant in jest, hung awkwardly in the air as Kuşien’s smile instantly faltered. His obliviousness to her discomfort spurred him on before he suddenly added, “It was the same with Hadrian…” He trailed off, catching the sharp, icy stare Kuşien fixed on him. His voice dwindled into a tense silence. From beside us, Kunnebudo, who had been watching the exchange with a hint of confusion, chimed in. “Even I know not to stir those waters, Taokar." she said, slightly reproaching. Taokar, now realising his mistake, scratched the back of his head, his expression turning earnest as he tried to explain. “I just meant... Hadrian and I were good friends, that’s all. And it’s the same now with Caelan. We jest amongst ourselves as friends do, no harm meant.” Kuşien was still silent, her orange eyes unblinking. “Only friendly banter, truly,” he added, his voice softer, attempting to mend the gap his words had created. Kuşien’s expression softened slightly but remained guarded. She nodded slowly, signalling a cautious acceptance of his explanation, though the earlier warmth between us had cooled slightly. “I’m sorry." he murmured, his usual robust voice now quiet. He cast a quick, uncertain glance at Kuşien’s serious face before retreating back to the celebration’s heart, his large frame disappearing among the villagers. 
Kunnebudo, sensing the tension, gently took my arm and guided me away from the scene. “Let’s bring the translator back to the centre,” she suggested. “Everyone should be able to talk freely without thinking too much about the languages.” As we walked, the village lights danced in her bright eyes, reflecting a mix of concern and nostalgia. “Taokar always loved teasing Kuşien, even as kids. It’s his way, you know? But when Hadrian came to live with them, it was much the same for him at first.” Her voice took on a reflective note. “Taokar did not spare him either. But, you see, Hadrian had this charm, this patience, he soon turned those teasings into friendship.” She paused, letting the sounds of laughter and music from the celebration fill the space between her words. “Manmurekan and I are from different tribes. There was a time when their chieftain's daughter, Huzur, who is very forward-thinking, started a cultural interchange programme. She believed that sharing knowledge strengthens all tribes. Huzur was the one who invited Hadrian to settle with us.” Kunnebudo continued, her voice lowering almost into reverence. “She wanted him to share his knowledge with everyone. We were like his pupils, Kuşien, Manmurekan and I. He taught Kuşien how to use a bow. You should have seen her the first day, aim all awry. But Hadrian was patient, always guiding her hands until she mastered it. He taught her how to read and write in Sendralese. She developed under his guidance and they were always together.” Kunnebudo said, her tone filled with nostalgia. “That’s why it hit her hard when he... passed." She paused, gauging my reaction. "It was sudden. He was stabbed in the back by mercenaries. And now, having someone around who reminds her so much of him, it’s like reopening a wound every time she sees you.”
What else could I say? Still taking me by the arm, she led me towards a central table, upon which I placed the area translator back. The meaningless chatter of the people around us became intelligible. "She needs some time, doesn't she?" I asked. "How long has it been since Hadrian parted?" Forcing her memory, Kunnebudo led a finger to her lips. "A little over a year, I believe." I remembered how devastated my father was when mother died. I have had two or three lovers in the past but none of them had their lives cut short, much less by such a violent means. I can only imagine the feeling. Suddenly, Kunnebudo grabbed my hand. I became flustered and probably blushed as she brought it closer to her face and began examining it. "Such delicate fingernails you have. I had never noticed it before but our fingernails are different. See?" She showed me her hand and I indeed noticed a difference. The nails on her four-fingered hand were darker and thicker, definitely more resistant. As she grinned, I also noticed her canine teeth were sharper and slightly longer. How did I miss such details until now? Thinking about it well, our other companions also had these characteristics. Leave it to Kunnebudo to be so spontaneous and to change the subject so abruptly.
Kunnebudo’s golden eyes crinkled at the corners as she laughed again. As she stood close, her arm brushed mine, her fingers lingering just a moment longer than usual. It must have been an accidental brush since we were in a quite crowded place. “We’ve had our fill of rest and food, haven’t we?” Manmurekan’s voice broke through the villagers' noises as she approached. “It’s time to gather our belongings. I’ll fetch Kuşien and Taokar. We ought to regroup at the inn and prepare to leave before midday.” I nodded in agreement. Kunnebudo talked briefly with an elder, asking to borrow the area translator again so that we could plan our journey and quickly steered us towards the inn to start packing. The walk back was brief, filled with her lively chatter about the exotic foods (to her, at least) we had eaten. Once back, Kunnebudo and I started organizing our gear in the quiet of the inn, our companions temporarily absent. As we packed, Kunnebudo's tone shifted, her voice lowering slightly as she ventured into more personal territory. “You know, the Hazrun don’t look at relationships quite as your people do… We have only about a week or so each year when we can conceive, and only with our own kind.” She explained, her gaze thoughtful as she folded her clothing. “This has shaped our views quite liberally about casual relationships, which are less frowned upon.”
She paused a moment, her eyes lifting to meet mine, a curious tilt to her head. “I often wonder what else might be different between our races, appearance-wise… Although, Kuşien and Hadrian were a couple, weren’t they? It must not be all that significant.” The mention of Kuşien and Hadrian momentarily drew my thoughts away, pondering the details of relationships between different races and how such unions were perceived by different cultures. I nodded, somewhat absent-mindedly, as I packed my own bag. I had never seen a Hazrun's nude body, though I assumed they were similar, if not identical, to the other races. Humans, Renshi, Hazrun, Sulcai, Usagzok, Anglo-Elves, Elves, and Mustalf all have minor anatomical differences, though nothing so significant to prevent... let's say, nature to take its course. Just then, the rest of our group entered the room, Manmurekan leading with haste, Kuşien’s eyes slightly downcast and Taokar’s usual energy filling the space. Kunnebudo’s demeanour shifted abruptly, her previous words seeming to hang awkwardly between us, her cheeks tinged with a faint blush as she turned her attention quickly back to her packing.
Kuşien glanced over, her expression unreadable, and Kunnebudo smiled quickly, a tight, polite curve of her lips that didn’t quite reach her eyes. The room filled with the sounds of the rustling of bags, each of us lost in our own thoughts as we prepared for the next leg of our journey. We then returned the area translator to a Sulcai village elder, who expressed his gratitude by presenting me with a letter sealed with wax, the seal's design being the crest of the Temple of Ma'at: three circles inside a pentagonal shape. “This letter is for you, human,” the elder explained while the translator's effect was still active. “Give to a priest so that your business gets priority.” Grateful for his generous offer, I slid it carefully into my pack. 
The group began to follow a lesser-known path shown only on an old map from the village as a shortcut to the main temple road. However, we encountered the remnants of a recent landslide blocking our way. Taokar cursed in Hazrunic, disappointment evident from his furrowed brows. Kunnebudo sighed, settling to the ground to unwrap some provisions, while Kuşien stood a bit farther off, her eyes scanning the horizon, perhaps looking for alternative paths we could take.
Manmurekan, however, remained undeterred by the obstacle. Retrieving a small vial from her pack, she held up a bluish liquid, which I assumed was a potion of some sort. She explains in simple Hazrunic words, “Fire combines with thunder to make great explosion. I need more magic, great energy waste.” I watched as she uncorked the vial with a pop, downing the potion in a single, swift gulp. Her hands began to move through a series of complex, flowing hand signs, which were but one of the ways of spellcasting. I had seen this form only a few times, since most Anglo-Elf mages used verbal incantations instead. With a final sharp gesture, a surge of energy burst from her palms. The explosion that followed was tremendous, echoing off the mountains with a roar that momentarily stunned us all. Rocks and debris were blasted aside, leaving a jagged, but passable, path through the landslide. Breathless and dizzy, Manmurekan staggered, her strength faltering. Instinctively, I moved closer, offering my shoulder for support. “Put me down on the ground slowly,” she instructed. This seemed like mana depletion sickness, caused, as its name implies, by a complete depletion of one's mana reservoir. The only symptom she lacked was the characteristic pallor made unnoticeable by her stark white skin.
Gently, I eased her onto the rough ground, where she reclined with shut eyes, her chest rising and falling rapidly as she regained her strength. Taokar stepped forward, his expression a blend of concern and respect, offering to carry her along the way, but she waves him off with a weary hand. “Just… a moment,” she murmured. The rest of us took this unexpected break as an invitation to rest and eat. We shared some of the food that would expire earlier, such as fresh fruit and pastries we received from the village. After a considerable amount of time, Manmurekan’s breath steadied, and her eyes flicked open with renewed vigour. “Let’s continue” she declared, pushing herself up.
Moving along the path created by the landslide, we walked quickly, conscious of the diminishing light. As we approached a ridge and the land opened up, the main temple of Ma’at and its surrounding city came into view, impressive and distant, lit by the last rays of the sun. The time spent clearing the landslide and waiting for Manmurekan’s recovery meant we’d lost precious daylight. Standing there, with the city so near yet still a considerable distance on foot, we faced a decision as the sun set. Without the area translator, their discussions in Hazrunic were hard for me to follow in full, but I understood enough. They were debating whether to press on by night or to set up camp without a fire to remain hidden. Looking towards me, Kuşien’s urgent voice cut through, “You know more about this nation. Will we be safe?” I shook my head, feeling a pang of guilt for never paying closer attention to my mother’s stories of her pilgrimages. I could only reply uncertainly, “I'm not sure.” That settled it. We decided to camp right there for the night, without a fire to avoid attracting attention. Taokar immediately took charge of our safety, his large axe in hand, asserting, "Nothing will happen during my watch" with a convincing tone.
We set up our sparse camp in a natural hollow, which gave us some cover from the wind and any prying eyes. While Kuşien and Kunnebudo arranged our sleeping rolls, I helped quietly, my thoughts nervously circling around potential dangers lurking in the darkness. When I laid down and closed my eyes, I couldn't stop thinking about the few things I remembered from my mother's tales. She said we should be like Ma'at, who betrayed her own race and family to protect millions of people who owed nothing to her. I faintly remembered an illustration from a book she read to me and my sisters. An exotic looking girl, crimson-skinned and white-haired, held out her hands in front of a colossal pillar that stretched to the skies. This was probably a representation of her creating one of the Five Pillars. I couldn't help but fixate on the third eye on her forehead. Suddenly, she turned towards me, all eyes closed save for the third one, its sclera blue and its iris a pure white. Was I in control of my thoughts? Perhaps I drifted into sleep and was now dreaming. As she reached out to me, her arm slowly crumbled. Next was her entire head, with only one of the eyes remaining floating in place. It was eerie to look at that partial body. I noticed I was breathing heavily and was unable to move, symptoms I assumed to be of the so-called sleep paralysis.
A gentle hand then shook my shoulder and I could finally open my eyelids and return to the waking world. It was Manmurekan, who examined me with a mix of curiosity and distress. "Disturbed?" She said. "Bad sleep. No problem." I answered with my incomplete mastery of Hazrunic. Manmurekan giggled. "You had a 'towaimehe'. That means bad vision during sleep." I deduced that could only mean 'nightmare'. I sat up to look at the rest of the group. Taokar's bulky figure laid on an improvised mattress made of leaves, straw, and fabric on the ground, his limbs spread like a starfish. He was already sleeping, so I deduced I had slept for some hours and it was another person's shift. Manmurekan patted my back. "Sleep. You won't need to guard. Just be ready to heal when needed." Easier said than done. I lied down soon after, yet sleep eluded me. A mix of concern over my nightmare and anxiety due to being so close to fulfilling my promise prevented me from relaxing. Time crawled to a snail's pace as I waited for the sunrise. When the faintest light of dawn finally crept over the horizon, I awakened. As the light spread, the group stirred, and soon we were on our feet, packing our belongings. Today, my journey would either find its closure or prolong its purpose, and my heart raced with every step toward the grand temple city of Ma’at. Along the way, we encountered other pilgrims, each drawn by their own reasons to this sacred place.
At the city’s gates, I presented the letter from the village elder. The guards glanced over it, nodded, and led us to a registration booth where our names were recorded with no delay. Entering the city, we were struck by its grandeur. The temple of Ma’at tower tracks and the buildings around it were large and well-constructed, with the main temple visible at the city’s center, towering above everything else. The area was alive with activity; pilgrims prayed at shrines, and vendors sold food and religious items. However, our focus was on the massive temple ahead. Its doors were adorned with geometrical patterns and the symbol of her faith, three circles surrounded by a pentagon. "It is nearly time." Manmurekan noted. "The end of your duty to your mother." We advanced through the crowded streets, taking in the bustling activities around us. People from every race walked about, some in awe, obviously pilgrims, and others moving with purpose and used to the rhythm of the city, probably residents.
As we walked, we got closer to the vastness and architectural marvels of the main temple, a blend of sanctity and art. The structure’s spires reached skyward, and the intricate carvings illustrated Ma’at’s divine exploits. At the entrance, a priest greeted us, holding an area translator for convenience. He studied the village chief’s letter with a composed expression, nodding occasionally before addressing us. “Welcome, pilgrim Caelan,” he began, his voice serene yet authoritative. “You may enter. However, your companions, not being related to the ashes you carry, cannot join you beyond this point.” My companions exchanged uncertain glances but nodded in understanding. They murmured words of encouragement and good wishes before finding a place to wait among other pilgrims. The priest escorted me through enormous doors into the temple’s interior, where ethereal light filtered through stained glass windows, depicting various moments of Ma’at’s legend. As we proceeded, I noticed vivid imagery of a three-eyed girl with white hair and crimson skin, all her eyes serenely closed. This, I recognised, was a representation of Ma’at herself. Strangely similar to what I saw on my dream.
The priest began recounting her story as we walked deeper into the sacred halls. “Ma’at, once used as a tool by the Theoclasts, witnessed the devastation wrought upon the lands and defected, joining forces with the people of Yuandi. Her divine powers healed the land and erected the Five Pillars to maintain the Barrier. These acts solidified her place as a protector and healer deity revered by many.” Upon reaching a beautifully adorned chamber, the priest turned to me. “The village elder’s letter speaks highly of you and your companions. Your aid in dealing with the beast and healing those in need did not go unnoticed. For your service, I shall seek permission from higher authorities to allow you to witness the Holy Corpse of Ma’at herself.” Just as the priest finished, a voice echoed from behind us. “There is no need to request a permit. I will guide him there.” Turning, I saw a Sulcai woman of ethereal beauty. Her long green hair cascaded over her pristine white robes, and her deep blue eyes held an almost magnetic familiarity. “As you wish, Archbishop Solène,” the priest said, bowing respectfully.
Archbishop Solène was the second highest authority of the Ma’at faith, so that's likely why I felt that she was familiar. Her presence here at this specific moment seemed more than a coincidence somehow. “Follow me,” Solène instructed, her voice a mellow undertone of serene authority. As we navigated the temple’s labyrinthine passageways, it felt as though space itself distorted, the walls bending and swaying in almost psychedelic twists. This was some form of spatial or illusion magic to protect the Corpse, I reckoned. We stopped before an imposing, closed sarcophagus, majestically adorned and appearing as if it defied time itself. “Even in the afterlife,” Solène began, “the soul to whom those ashes belonged must feel overjoyed to be in Ma’at’s presence.”
I couldn't find the words. I'll admit I'm not a follower of the Ma'at faith but my eyes began to tear up. I could see Solène smiling softly. "Make no mistake, child. This occasion was preordained." I looked at her again, this time her face seemed more serious. "You saw visions in your dreams, didn't you?" She inquired. "Those about the Five Pillars and Ma'at disappearing?" I asked, deciding to not waste any time with minor details. She nodded solemnly. "Precisely. I am like you. You bear a fragment of Ma'at's essence. That is why you thought I looked familiar." I had heard of Ma'at's essence spreading or dissipating when she exhausted her divine powers after creating the Barrier and there indeed were some historical figures who accredited their success to this essence. "So... What's the reason for you leading me here?" "To return to the Holy Corpse the fragment that you bear." Her ocean-blue eyes were unrelenting. "What will change if I lose the fragment?" I started. "I assume I won't die or change too much, correct?" Solène continued to stare, this time as if analysing me. "I feel it within you. Your... affinity to light magic will very likely disappear." Which means I'd become useless if I were to return the fragment. I'm not strong, agile, intimidating, or intelligent enough to be useful. Healing is all I have!
"Fear not. Once all essences are united, Ma'at will reawaken. It will be a true rebirth of the goddess." I was still reluctant. Sensing my indecision, she continued: "As a demigoddess, the control of her divine half was imperfect, since she spent thousands of years imprisoned by the Theoclasts being used as a source of energy. Upon doing all she did for the people of Yuandi, her body and essence fractured. The fragments of her essence then randomly attached to thousands of other souls. You and I are among those." "How do you know all this?" I asked, skeptical and unconsciously ignoring her authority as the archbishop. Unexpectedly, she began unbuttoning the top of her robes. It was unthinkable that she was going to strip right before me, so I averted my eyes. "I understand your embarassment, but it's not what you think." I turned my head, seeing what looked like a blue light pulsing under the skin of her chest.
"That... W-why are you showing me..." I stuttered. "This is the Heart of Ma'at. A part of the Holy Corpse merged with me, giving me access to part of her memories." Solène explained. Just as Solène finished speaking, a quiet, grating sound filled the chamber. We both turned to witness the lid of the sarcophagus shifting slightly, a shadowy figure coming into view. Cloaked in a tattered hood, the intruder was completely wrapped in rags and bandages, giving the eerie appearance of an embalmed cadaver. Its hands were placed on the mummified Holy Corpse, a scene both jarring and blasphemous. Before we could react, the hooded figure, with a swift, almost preternatural motion, detached the arm and the head of the Holy Corpse. “Stop!” Solène shouted, her voice laced with desperation. But the thief paid no heed, clutching the sacred body parts and escaping as effortlessly as it had appeared. No barrier, no enchantment seemed to deter it, the spells designed to protect the Holy Corpse having no visible effect.
Solène stood aghast, her composure shattered. “It cannot be,” she muttered, grasping at the air as though she could pull the thief back. “To bypass such a powerful illusion spell…” Her eyes widened, trembling slightly. “A homunculus,” she whispered, more to herself than to me. “Only a being specifically created for immunity to illusions could accomplish this. I can't believe the Patriarch would let this possibility slip by.” Without missing another beat, Solène turned to me, urgency blazing in her eyes. “Caelan, I must act swiftly and I can't leave you here. Follow me!” She started back through the labyrinthine corridors, her steps echoing with urgency. As we emerged into the hall where the same priest stood waiting, his eyes widened and confused, she quickly briefed him about the situation and issued her commands crisply. “Spread the notice at once. Ensure the city gates are closed immediately. We must not allow the thief to escape.” Unused to such high stakes, I could only watch as a possibly historic event unfolded in front of me. Solène and the priest parted ways with haste, a turmoil forming as the alarm bells began to chime. Amidst the commotion, a small, spherical object on the ground caught my eye. It seemed almost inconspicuous, lying there in the chaos, but when I bent down to examine it, a chill ran down my spine.
The sphere was an eyeball, uncannily resembling the eye I’d seen in my dream: a blue sclera with a white iris. My breath caught in my throat, and I delicately wrapped it in a piece of cloth from my pocket, thinking, “I better hold on to that.” Intrigued and disturbed, I moved quickly, my mind racing with unanswered questions. Exiting the temple, I made my way back through the crowded streets to where my companions waited. Their expressions were a mixture of concern and curiosity, sensing immediately that something was amiss. I took a calming breath and started to brief them on what had transpired to my best knowledge of Hazrunic. "Ma'at's body was stolen. Arm and head run away." The city gates then clanged shut, sealing off any escape routes. Guards moved quickly among puzzled pilgrims, urging them to gather in designated open places such as squares and wide streets.
I could feel the tension in the air as we complied, making our way to a crowded square. The murmurs of confusion and concern from the assembled masses filled the air like a buzzing hive. Kuşien, keen-eyed as always, scanned our surroundings, her gaze landing on the guards searching through the belongings of others. I felt a cold sweat break out across my back. The Eye of Ma’at was still in my pocket, its presence gnawing at my insides. I couldn’t help but fidget as panic began to overtake me. What if they found it? What possible explanation could I offer? Kuşien’s sharp eyes darted towards me, her brow furrowing in concern. “Caelan,” she said softly in Hazrunic, “Are you alright?” I couldn’t bring myself to answer, my growing anxiety smothering any attempt at composure. I could feel the glances of my companions, each one a silent question of worry and confusion. A guard noticed my uneasiness and began walking towards us. My heart felt like a trapped bird beating against my ribcage. He was a stocky, grim-faced Renshi, and his gaze settled on me with a piercing scrutiny. As he got closer, he spoke aided by the area translator. “You, human. Come with me.” His tone brooked no argument.
I followed him reluctantly, casting a last, desperate look at my companions. “Wait here,” I managed to say, my voice shaking as I tried to put on a brave face for them. The guard led me to a temporary station set up for inspections. His eyes, still fixed intently on me, seemed to bore into my very soul. “I was informed that a human was nearby when the parts of the Holy Corpse were stolen,” he said, his voice as cold as the steel of his armour. “I… I didn’t...” My words caught in my throat, my mind racing. Before I could formulate a coherent response, he began searching my pack. He pulled out the contents, meticulously examining each item. A lump of dread rose in my throat. His inspection of my pack complete with no incriminating evidence found, the guard turned his attention to me, his gaze even more scrutinising. He reached into my pockets. My breath hitched as his hand closed around something small and spherical… but with a puzzled expression, he pulled out only a small, intricately carved wooden trinket I had bought from the village where we stayed the day before. Perhaps noticing my relief, he softened slightly. “It seems my suspicions were misplaced. Perhaps you’re tense because of the situation, not because you did something wrong. I’m sorry, pilgrim.” His apology was brief, but sincere, and he gestured for me to step aside as he called for my companions to be searched as well.
I joined the others, my mind still reeling. The Eye of Ma’at… where had it gone? What had happened back in the temple? As the guards finished with my companions and moved on, Taokar gave me a questioning look. “What happened? Your skin is as pale as Manmurekan’s.” I took a deep breath, gathering myself. “I had… the Eye of Ma’at in my pocket. Now it vanished.” Their faces reflected a mix of disbelief and concern. Kuşien’s eyes narrowed as she leaned closer, her voice a whisper. “Vanished? How?” “The guard couldn’t find it,” I replied, my voice barely above a murmur. “I don’t know.”
Hours passed, and the guards’ exhaustive search continued to yield nothing. The sun was beginning to set, casting long shadows across the stone-paved streets of the temple city. I overheard snippets of conversation from the guards nearby, one of them muttering to another, “Still nothing to report. It’s like the thief vanished into thin air.” We had been corralled in the designated square all day, the atmosphere heavy with tension and murmurs of concerned pilgrims. My Hazrun companions spoke to each other in low tones, their language gradually becoming less alien to me. I felt a small sense of triumph amidst the chaos; I was beginning to understand their words more each day. Suddenly, a jolt of realisation hit me. My mother’s ashes! They were left unattended in the reliquary. Panic surged before a calm rationale settled in. They were already so close to Ma’at; surely, I had fulfilled my mother’s last wish beyond even her wildest hopes. As I scanned the crowd, my eyes fell upon Solène. She stood some distance away but was unmistakably pointing in our direction. A group of guards quickly broke through the sea of pilgrims, making their way towards us.
“You and your companions are required inside the main temple,” one of them said, his tone leaving no room for argument. We followed them back to the temple’s imposing structure. The echoing hallways felt familiarly unsettling this time, leading me to wonder about the gravity of the situation awaiting us. The guards finally led us into a richly adorned chamber where Solène awaited, seated behind a large table littered with papers and letters. An area translator sat among them, flickering softly. Despite it being less than ten hours since I last saw her, Solène looked like she hadn’t slept in days. Her eyes were shadowed with exhaustion, her brow furrowed with stress. “There is nothing more we can do immediately,” Solène began, her voice tinged with frustration and despair. “We’ve sent out search parties across the continent, but catching the thief or their beneficiaries will be immensely challenging and time-consuming.” Suddenly, her gaze sharpened, fixing intensely on me. Leaning forward, she scrutinised my face as if she could see through me. Kuşien and Taokar tensed up, moving protectively closer, but she raised a hand to calm them as she sat back in her chair.
“Now we’re even more alike, Caelan,” she said, her tone carrying an eerie certainty. “I can feel it within you. You have merged with the Eye of Ma’at.” The revelation hung in the air, leaving everyone stunned. I felt a mix of confusion and disbelief. “Merged?” I managed to stammer. The situation seemed even more dire now. But there was a glint of light in Solène’s eyes as an idea began to form. “This may actually be to our advantage,” she murmured, almost to herself before addressing the room. “Caelan, since you have merged with a part of the Holy Corpse, you may be able to sense the presence of other parts as I did now.” Knowing what she was implying, a tremor of realisation ran through me. “You mean, I can help find the rest?” “You can,” Solène affirmed, her voice resolute. “Though I suspect only from up close, unless someone uses the divine power of the Corpse.” The weight of it all settled on my shoulders. I had initially come here to fulfill a last request, but fate had drafted me into something far grander and more dangerous.
“Will you help us, Caelan?” Solène asked, her tired eyes pleading for my aid. I glanced at my companions, each one giving a nod of encouragement. "I don't think I have a choice. But I'm afraid someone might misuse the power of Ma'at, so I agree." Solène sighed in relief. I noticed a faint glow coming from her chest. Curious, I turned to Manmurekan, who stood by my side. “Can you see that glow from her chest?” I whispered. Manmurekan shook her head slowly. “No, Caelan. I have no mana sight, and even if I did, mana typically spreads throughout the body. It’s strange for it to concentrate in only one place.”
Solène nodded. “Indeed. What you’re seeing is the Heart of Ma’at within me. I can feel the Eye of Ma’at within you, as well as sense if someone bears one of the countless fragments of her essence. You might experience unexpected changes or see glimpses of Ma’at’s memories, particularly during sleep.” I felt a shiver run down my spine. “What kind of changes can I expect?” Solène’s expression softened. “I cannot say for sure. You are the fourth person to merge with a part of the Holy Corpse, and each experienced different effects. We’ll need to be vigilant.” “How were the parts returned?” I inquired. “The corresponding body part has to be physically removed,” Solène replied solemnly. “So eventually, you will have to return your eye to Ma’at.” The thought made my stomach churn. I glanced at Solène and realised that she, too, would lose her heart when the time came. With resolve, I then remembered the promise I had made to Manmurekan. “Before we start searching, we must visit Manmurekan’s village.”
Manmurekan’s eyes glistened with gratitude. “Thank you, Caelan.” Solène nodded approvingly. “Since you will be in Jirkaeriya, you can begin searching there. We have heard rumours of disturbances on the Black Pillar. The timing could not be more fortuitous.” As I absorbed this information, I realised I needed to contact my family, to let them know I wouldn’t be home for an indeterminate amount of time. “May I write a letter to my family?” I asked Solène. She agreed with a warm smile. “I will ensure it is delivered. Thank you for your willingness to help, Caelan. As a fellow ‘blessed one,’ I am counting on you.”
With a heavy heart, I penned a letter to my family, crafting a story to keep them from worrying. While I wrote, my companions conversed among themselves. I could hear Taokar’s deep voice murmuring with determination. “We have to support Caelan. Maybe he can even help end the war with Igirith.” Kuşien’s voice held a note of skepticism. “It’s not our concern. We should just stick to Solène’s orders. The Archbishopric has always been a neutral nation.” Taokar’s voice grew more intense, a touch of anger lacing his words. “Do you not wish for the war to end? Our village was razed by this conflict.” Kuşien fell silent, and I could see her clenching her fists. Taokar’s next words hit hard. “Remember, Kuşien. Hadrian was killed by Anglo-Elves.” Kuşien stuttered, her voice barely above a whisper. “I-I… leave that decision to Caelan.” With that, she excused herself and left the room hastily. Kunnebudo cast a sidelong glance at Taokar before following Kuşien wordlessly. I watched them leave, feeling a pang of sorrow for Kuşien’s unresolved grief. It was clear Kunnebudo went to comfort her. Turning back to my letter, I finished writing it and handed it over to Solène. “I’ll do what I can.”
As we left Solène’s office, the gravity of our new mission weighed heavily upon me. At the end of the grand hallway, I spotted Kuşien and Kunnebudo. Kunnebudo had an arm draped over her friend’s back, offering what comfort she could. Taokar briefly turned back to Manmurekan and me. “I’ll wait outside,” he stated simply before turning on his heel and disappearing down the hall, walking past Kunnebudo and Kuşien and apparently pretending to ignore them. Still within the translator’s range, Manmurekan’s voice broke the silence, carrying a hint of melancholy. “We may be childhood friends, but even we have our issues.” Her eyes bore into mine. “Taokar cares deeply about this war, no matter how boisterous he appears. His two older brothers and father were drafted two years ago and never returned. Now it’s just him and his sister, trying to keep their clan’s legacy alive.” I could feel the heaviness in her voice. She paused, gathering her thoughts. “As for me… Seeing my family again after so long, I don’t know how I’ll react. The hope is that I’ll have the strength to leave them once more and continue travelling with you all. That is, if the Death Runners haven’t already taken their souls.” I leaned in slightly, my voice gentle yet firm. “You don’t have to decide anything for now, Manmurekan. Your company has been invaluable, but I won’t press the issue." Our eyes met, and for the first time, I noticed subtle details about her; the delicate curve of her lips, the contrast between her jet-black hair and her pale, almost ghostly skin, the way her red eyes glimmered with strength... Realising I had stared too long, I coughed awkwardly and changed the subject. “What exactly are the Death Runners?”
"They are the servants of the Moon Goddess Naicin,” she explained, her eyes distant as if recalling a long-told tale. “They guide the souls of the deceased Hazrun to the moon at night.” I pondered this for a moment, finding it fascinating that the moon was their equivalent to our underworld. Manmurekan glanced back at Kuşien and Kunnebudo, who still huddled together at the end of the hall. “We must start somewhere.” she said with resolve. “After visiting my village, we should head to the capital. Huzur Tartsusime, the wife of the Soho, might be able to help us.” The name clicked in my memory, and I asked, “Wasn’t Huzur the daughter of the chieftain of Kuşien’s village?” Manmurekan nodded. “Yes. She's part of a distant provincial branch of the current ruling family. Tazkiairga Jadaera, the current Soho, chose her as his wife in a political maneuver to counterbalance the power of the more traditional and established clans when he was vying for leadership. Now that he is ill and bedridden, Huzur effectively governs the confederacy.” “So, she’s a powerful ally,” I concluded. “Indeed,” Manmurekan affirmed. “But she’s also someone we trust. Old ties can sometimes mean more than politics.”
As we approached Kuşien and Kunnebudo, the latter subtly gestured for us to pause, her hand raising in a faint but unmistakable sign. Her whispered words carried through the hallway, though they weren’t decipherable enough for me to catch every one of them. I did manage to piece together some terms. I presumed her message was something along the lines of “she should not see the human for now.” A pang of guilt hit me. I had thought Kuşien’s trauma was deep, but I clearly underestimated its extent. Turning to Manmurekan with a shared look of understanding, we made our way outside. Taokar leaned casually against a stone wall, his posture one of feigned indifference. Catching sight of us, he straightened. “Manmurekan...” Taokar began, but she cut him off with a gentle but firm hand on his shoulder. “You two need some time away. Walk around the city and clear your minds. We will wait for you in front of the temple.” He glanced at me, and despite the concern in his golden eyes, he nodded reluctantly. As we wandered through the twilit city, the atmosphere remained heavy with the apprehension of the recent theft. Wisps of conversation reached us from worried pilgrims and vigilant guards. The streets, while busy, seemed oddly silent. For a while, we walked in silence, Taokar’s usual demeanour replaced by a contemplative quiet. I felt the weight of his thoughts and decided to initiate a conversation, even with my limited Hazrunic.
“Is family important to your people?” I asked. Taokar gave a slight nod, his gaze fixed on the cobbled street. “My family… all warriors. Father and older brothers… gone. I am left.” He sighed deeply, the air escaping his lungs like the burden weighed heavily on his soul. “I wish I was firstborn, then I would have gone to war. Not be left behind…” “Do you… think they are still fighting?” I asked, my voice low, mindful of the potential grief in my question. “Dead or fighting still. I know not,” he replied. “Only my sister left. Married off to a man… north, away from the war.” Thinking about the war raised emotions in Taokar. His hands clenched into fists, knuckles white. “The Red-Hairs must pay for death! Greed! They want two pillars. The Red Pillar isn’t enough. They want the Black Pillar from us.” he seethed, his anger more pronounced than I had ever seen.
Understanding his rage, I sought a way to ease it. “War is a tragic thing. Perhaps Huzur… when we reach the capital… she can clarify,” I offered, my words hopeful yet uncertain. “We must find reasons for Anglo-Elf aggression. Reasons we do not know.” To my surprise, Taokar’s expression softened, and he chuckled, albeit mirthlessly. “You truly remind me of Hadrian. Optimistic… always looking for peace.” As we continued to walk through the twilight-draped city, I couldn’t help but reflect on the strange path my life had taken. If I had been born an Anglo-Elf like my foster family, I would never have encountered this group. This was a secret they could never know. My loyalty to Igirith was small, but my love for my family and my village was strong. They shouldn’t suffer for the kingdom’s mistakes. Taokar rekindled his smile and gave me a hearty pat on the back. “Enough walk, Caelan. Stars in sky now,” he said in Hazrunic, pointing upward. His finger traced the faintly glowing constellations that were beginning to appear. It was then I realized the word he used for ‘star’ was the same as Kuşien’s name.
We returned to the temple steps where Kuşien, Kunnebudo, and Manmurekan were sitting. Kuşien averted her gaze when she saw us approaching, while Taokar’s previous guilt resurfaced momentarily before he offered a nod in her direction. Seeking to lighten the mood, I pointed to the sky, saying in my hesitant Hazrunic, “I learnt that your name means ‘star’.” Her eyes flickered briefly up at me, her lips slightly curling into a smile, but she quickly looked away again. Kunnebudo, chimed in. She pointed to a dark cloud overhead, mimicking the noise of thunder. “My name is ‘Black Cloud.’ I was born during a storm.” she explained, a mischievous smile playing on her lips. Her infectious energy drew everyone’s attention. Manmurekan and Taokar followed suit, both offering explanations for their names. Manmurekan pointed southwards. “My name, ‘South Wind.’ After a mythical guardian of the south.” she said, her voice a gentle breeze itself. Taokar, with a hint of pride, said, “My name means ‘Long Thread.’ My parents wished a long life for me.” His smile faltered momentarily, perhaps realising the significance of his name, but it returned quickly as they all turned to me, curiosity evident in their eyes.
“And you, Caelan?” Kunnebudo asked, her golden eyes shimmering with interest. “What's the meaning of yours?” I hesitated, feeling the weight of their expectant gazes. “I’m not sure,” I admitted. “I was named after an ancestor. My family never told me much about him.” A short silence followed. Kuşien, despite her earlier reluctance, finally let herself participate in the conversation. “Each name holds a story. Your ancestor’s story may be unknown to you, but you carry it.” she said quietly, almost as if speaking to herself. Kunnebudo suddenly seemed to remember something. She rummaged through her satchel and pulled out a badge with an elaborate crest featuring the pentagon and three spheres. “Solène sent this through a priest,” handing it to Manmurekan with an apologetic smile. “For shelter in temples when travelling. Solène apologised for not being able to help more.”
Manmurekan examined the badge, her expression softening into one of relief. “This will be useful tonight,” she said. “Since it’s already dark, we can use it to find a place to rest.” Nodding in agreement, we set off towards another temple closer to the city’s outskirts so that we could quickly leave once the sun rose. The earlier tension between Taokar and Kuşien lingered in the air, making the journey silent and somewhat heavy. We arrived at the smaller temple and presented the badge to an attendant, who quickly moved to make arrangements for our stay. He handed me a parchment and quill, clearly indicating that we should write our names. Observing my confusion, Kuşien gently took the quill from my hand. With swift, practiced movements, she wrote down all their names in the human alphabet before passing the parchment back to me. “Kuşien Ontzuwa, Manmurekan Mahyerebai, Kunnebudo Nuoidukea, and Taokar Mirtahaunoz.” I read their full names in my mind, finding the Hazrun language both peculiar and fascinating. Then, I added my own name, 'Caelan Riáta' to the list before handing the document to the human clerk. He gestured for us to follow him.
The clerk led Taokar and me to a modest room, and the three women to another. Taokar flopped down onto one of the beds without bothering to change clothes or look through his pack, a weariness overtaking him. His head no sooner hit the pillow than he began snoring softly. I couldn’t help but smile at Taokar’s deep, immediate sleep. It was a comforting sound after such a tumultuous day, but it also made me slightly envious. I knew I would have trouble sleeping tonight. As I sorted through my items, laying out my clothes and gear, my mind whirled with thoughts of the day’s revelations and the path that lay ahead. I couldn’t shake the image of Solène standing in her office, the urgency in her eyes, or the unsettling, surreal dreamscape in which Ma’at had reached out to me. The weight of my responsibility settled onto my shoulders once more. As I finally laid down, I found myself staring up at the wooden beams of the ceiling, listening to Taokar’s steady breathing. I closed my eyes, knowing that sleep would eventually come, even if it was filled with more enigmatic visions.
I found myself drifting into sleep, exhaustion finally overcoming my thoughts. As my consciousness wavered, the dreamscape took hold, and suddenly, it was not my own memories I was reliving. Through Ma’at’s eyes, I found myself, or rather her, submerged in a strange, viscous liquid inside what looked like a glass casket. The world outside was an enigma of glimmering lights and metallic structures, all unfamiliar to me. The liquid was cold, surrounding her with an uncomfortable pressure, and I felt various wires and pipes snaking around and into her body. Her crimson skin, slick from the liquid, seemed eerily unfamiliar. From beyond the glass and blurry from the liquid's turbidity, I could see humanoid figures, though I couldn't discern any details. Were they the dreaded Theoclasts? They maneuvered around silently, fingers flying over strange, flat, glowing panels. The room beyond the glass was filled with the hums and noises of unknown artefacts and equipment. Ma’at’s vision shifted downward, looking through her own confined body. The sight of wires and tubes piercing her flesh incited a visceral feeling of dread and helplessness. Panic settled in as the liquid pressed tightly against her, providing no space to squirm free. She desperately tried to move but found herself immobilised, suspended within the contraption. A sharp flash of pain surged through me—I mean Ma’at—as one of the figures adjusted something on the machinery. The overwhelming terror and physical strain were too intense for Ma’at, causing her to feel faint. Darkness rapidly closed in as her vision dimmed, fading out the mysterious scene around her.
The intense pressure lifted suddenly, and I awoke with a start, gasping for breath and drenched in cold sweat. I instinctively touched various parts of my own body, half-expecting to find the same wires and pipes piercing my skin. The surreal fragment of Ma’at’s past left a mark on me. The muffled snores of Taokar beside me felt like they were from another world entirely, distant and unsure. The remainder of the night I spent restlessly, turning and waking multiple times. The fragments of Ma’at’s memory continued to swirl in my mind. When the first rays of dawn infiltrated the room, I felt far from well-rested. Taokar, however, was still lost in slumber, his snores echoing in the otherwise quiet room. I decided to let him sleep a bit longer and made my way to the room where the three women were staying. I knocked on the door, and after a few moments, Kunnebudo’s voice called out, giving me permission to enter. Pushing the door open, I found her still lying on the bed, her hair mussed and the covers in disarray. Despite her messy appearance, she greeted me with a warm smile. “Good morning.” “Good morning, Kunnebudo. Where are Kuşien and Manmurekan?” I asked, glancing around the room to find no trace of them. She shrugged slightly, her sleep-weighted eyes blinking slowly. “No idea. They left before I woke up.”
Kunnebudo, ever observant, caught my evidently tired look. “Did you not rest well?” she asked with genuine concern. “No,” I admitted, realizing that my limited grasp of Hazrunic wasn’t enough to describe the memories I’d relived. I decided it would be best to talk about it only when we had an area translator. “And you? You seem well-rested.” She stretched languidly, causing the cover to slip slightly, revealing more of her skin than I expected to see, namely her legs and stomach. I averted my eyes, feeling my face flush. “It’s been a long time since I haven’t had to sleep on the ground.” Noticing my reaction, she chuckled softly at my discomfort. “You would not last a second in a Keiozhazrun village during summer,” she said with amusement. “We wear very little clothing then.” I shifted awkwardly, trying to keep my gaze respectfully averted. After a few more seconds that felt like an eternity, Kunnebudo asked, “When was the last time you were close with a woman?” My face surely turned an even deeper shade of red. “It’s been quite a long time,” I admitted reluctantly. “I see,” she said thoughtfully. “You must feel stressed. You would sleep better if you felt the warmth of somebody else. You hornless ones cannot reproduce with us, so there's no need to worry.” “It’s more of a cultural concern, not a fear of pregnancy.” I replied.
She raised an eyebrow, clearly intrigued by my unease. “Hadrian wasn’t prude like you are,” she commented, making me question the differences between the upbringing of humans and if my Anglo-Elf foster family held stricter views. “That’s how my family raised me.” I replied.
