"Well, if you'll excuse me, I should check my pack to make sure everything's there." I awkwardly went back to my room and found Taokar still snoring softly. As I went through my belongings, my mind drifted back to the potential reactions of my companions if they discovered my true origin: the fact that I hailed from the enemy nation Igirith, despite not being an elf or an Anglo-Elf. It was a secret I would have to guard closely for now. I finished sorting my pack and decided to go downstairs in search of Kuşien and Manmurekan. The temple was quiet at this early hour, the only sounds being the distant murmur of priests and pilgrims beginning their day’s activities. Descending the stone steps, the air was cool and filled with the subtle scent of incense. As I entered the main hall, I caught sight of Kuşien engaged in conversation with the human clerk from last night. Nearby, Manmurekan busied herself scribbling on a piece of paper.
“Good morning.” Kuşien glanced up, offering a brief nod before resuming her conversation with the clerk, their voices low. Manmurekan looked up from her work and gave me a quick smile. “Morning, Caelan. We’re gathering information about the best way to my village. The roads to take, paths to avoid, where other temples are located…” Her tone was efficient, focused. “Is it far?” I asked. “Not as far as we expected.” Manmurekan replied. “The Damohazrun lands directly border the Archbishopric, though the path is mountainous and not easy to traverse.” She paused, studying my face with concern. “You don’t look too good, Caelan.” Realising I couldn’t hide my weariness, I nodded. “I had another nightmare. Not exactly that, but the words of your language elude me. We shall talk about it when we find an area translator.” Manmurekan’s gaze softened with understanding. “We’ll find one once everyone’s ready. For now, we need to finish preparing. Where are the other two?” “Taokar might still be sleeping. Kunnebudo had just woken up before I came here.”
Kuşien and the clerk concluded their conversation, and she turned toward us. “We have enough information to start our journey. Let’s go back upstairs and make sure we are all ready.” She spoke briskly, her expression a blend of impatience and focus. Her newly-obtained information gave us a clearer idea of the route we were to take, which made our departure feel all the more urgent. I let out a low sigh, mentally preparing myself for what lay ahead. Together, we made our way back upstairs. Taokar was still sprawled across his bed, snoring loudly. Kunnebudo had risen, though she wasn’t fully ready for the day. The conversation we had earlier still played in my mind, making the situation slightly awkward for me. Whether it lingered just as strongly in her thoughts, or if she was an excellent actor, I couldn’t tell. Manmurekan’s voice was authoritative yet gentle as she addressed Taokar. “Wake up, Taokar. We’re departing soon.” Groaning, he rolled onto his back before slowly sitting up, rubbing his eyes. “Yes, yes. I’m up now.” Kunnebudo noticed my entrance with a light smile framed by her sharp canines, although she didn’t comment on anything from earlier. I assisted Taokar in gathering his gear. As we finished packing, I occasionally glanced at Kunnebudo, wondering if any signs of our conversation would seep through her actions. I couldn’t gauge anything out of the ordinary. She was focused and efficient, treating our departure with the seriousness it deserved.
We left our rooms and traversed back into the main hall. As we moved toward the exit, the other patrons of the temple seemed somewhat distracted, their eyes shifting toward us occasionally, but more so toward priests who spoke in hushed tones. The theft of the Holy Corpse parts hadn’t been leaked to the public yet, but an air of unease lingered.
Passing through the city gates, the sounds of everyday life resumed around us in a somewhat muted tone. People mingled about, their actions betraying underlying anxiousness. At the sight of two Mustalf men and their horse wagon, it felt like a small victory. They were agreeable enough to give us a ride to Jirkaeriya. “We’re heading there to meet our caravan.” one of the Mustalf men explained. His name was Aldreon, his blue eyes glinting with both curiosity and guarded caution. His companion, Kaal, seemed more focused on the horses, giving them gentle pats and making sure they were well-settled. “Your Hazrunic is very good.” I remarked, my curiosity getting the better of me as we climbed onto the wagon. Aldreon cracked a smile. “We Mustalf wanderers need to speak several languages. We act as commerce intermediaries, even between warring nations like Jirkaeriya and Igirith.” Assuming he could speak my language, I switched to Anglo-Elven, “How’s the war situation these days?” Kaal looked up with a grave expression. “The Valaranalf are stubborn.” he said using the Mustalf term for elves, which literally meant 'Pyrite Elves' (i.e. 'Fool's Gold Elves') “They won’t negotiate for a peace treaty or even a simple truce.”
The atmosphere grew heavier as we journeyed forward, the tension from the war seeping into the newfound silence. The hours that followed were relatively quiet, the rhythmic swaying of the wagon providing an almost hypnotic lull. I found myself succumbing to the tranquil motion, my earlier restlessness giving way to exhaustion. Memories, or perhaps Ma’at’s memories, began to surface in my semi-conscious state. She was healing the wounds of a young Sulcai girl with green hair. Her vision seemed blurry, yet serene. The girl, her injuries mending under Ma’at’s gentle care, offered her a flower and a small piece of bread. “Eat!” she said with childlike enthusiasm. Instead of the bread, Ma’at took a bite from the flower, causing the little girl to laugh heartily, her innocence and joy palpable even in the vision. I awoke with a gentle, lingering smile, realising I had been leaning on Kuşien’s shoulder. Embarrassed, I quickly repositioned myself and apologised. Kuşien still didn’t meet my eyes, but her voice carried a hint of understanding. “It’s alright. You seemed very tired.” Across from us, Taokar watched with a half-smile, his earlier contemplative mood replaced with an amused glint. Kunnebudo was barely containing her laughter, her hand brushing her mouth to hide the smile breaking through.
Aldreon exchanged a few words with Taokar before turning back to me. His brow furrowed, a contemplative look crossing his face. “You know, human faces are so hard to distinguish… but you seem familiar somehow. Have we met before?” I nodded. “Perhaps. I travelled with a Mustalf caravan some time ago. Tethys and Elna were among them.” Kaal, still focused on the horses, let out a soft chuckle. “Ah, you're the healer. I knew I recognised you.” We shared a few more pleasantries as the wagon trudged along the rocky roads. Eventually, the familiar bustling sounds of a caravan camp reached our ears. As we rolled to a stop, familiar faces began to come into view. Elna spotted me first. Her red hair danced in the wind as she broke into a broad smile. Before I could even step off the wagon, she was upon me, enveloping me in a tight hug. “Caelan! I can’t believe you're back!” she exclaimed. I returned the hug with a warm smile. As we pulled apart, she ushered me towards a central tent. “You have to see Tethys. She’ll be thrilled!” Elna said, leading the way. As we entered the tent, Tethys looked up from a concoction she was working on. Her red eyes widened in surprise, and a smile spread across her face. “I didn’t expect to see you this far up north! What brings you here?” I introduced my Hazrun companions, who took in their surroundings with a mix of curiosity and caution. As they exchanged pleasantries, I caught up with Tethys and Elna, recounting my journey and our next destinations, careful not to mention anything about the Holy Corpse. Throughout our conversation, I couldn’t help but notice Kuşien standing a little apart, her gaze tightening each time Elna touched my arm or leaned in a bit too closely. Elna’s eyes twinkled with mischief as she asked, “So, Caelan, have you found someone yet?” Her voice was light, but there was a sincere curiosity behind her playful tone. Before I could respond, Tethys cut in, a wry smile on her face. “I could use your help gathering ingredients for a potion I’m working on. Are you up for it?” I nodded eagerly, grateful for the distraction, and followed Tethys, leaving the tense interaction behind. We ventured into a grove near the camp, discussing the differences between light and dark magic, sharing newfound knowledge and enjoying each other’s company.
Back at the camp, the Hazrun group interacted with the Mustalf. Many of them knew Hazrunic due to their frequent trade relations, and soon enough, animated conversations ensued. Taokar was seen charming a Mustalf woman with a booming laugh that echoed through the camp. At times, she shyly hid her face behind a curtain of blonde hair as he continued his light-hearted banter. As dusk settled, it became apparent that we would have to stay the night with the caravan. The hurry about reaching Manmurekan’s village was quietly set aside for the evening. We all felt we needed a break. The Mustalf set up a bonfire, and the night transformed into a small celebration, meant to welcome me back and entertain their Hazrun guests. The music began, lively and full of spirit. Elna danced her way through the camp, pulling me by the hand to join the festivities. Mustalf delicacies were passed around, each more exotic than the last. Manmurekan and Kunnebudo took up some skewered meat that was suspiciously red. I tried some myself but found the spice overwhelming, causing my face to flush and eyes to water. “Our species can’t feel spicy tastes.” Manmurekan explained with a laugh. “To us, it tastes the same as regular meat.” “Good to know." I said between gulps of water. A Mustalf man got into an accident during a sword dance, making an urgent call for a healer. Stepping up, I quickly cast a healing spell. The response was immediate and powerful, his wounds closing faster and more completely than I was used to. I blinked, realising my healing prowess had dramatically increased, surely due to Ma'at's influence. "What's that? Have you finally learnt higher level spells?" Tethys asked as I returned. I shrugged, not sure what to tell her. Touching her own chest, Elna asked: "Can your magic heal wounds of the heart?" Even if I had understood the intent behind the question, I spent some seconds thinking if light magic could indeed help people who have had heart attacks or heart failure. Elna raised an eyebrow as Tethys laughed at the interaction. Later, encouraged by the musical spirit of the celebration, someone called out to Kuşien, urging her to play the flute. She refused, her discomfort clear. Yet, as the insistence grew, she lashed out in frustration, her voice shaking. “No! I don’t want to! Can you not understand that?” she shouted, her sudden outburst stunning everyone into silence. A moment later, she seemed to realize her behaviour and muttered a quick apology before storming off.
I wanted to follow her, but before I could, Elna tugged at my arm, pulling me back towards the bonfire. “Come on, Caelan. Don’t let it ruin our night.” She led me to try more delicacies, urging me to join in the dances. Manmurekan and Kunnebudo focused on the festivities around them, enjoying the rare chance to indulge in some carefree revelry, though I could see them glancing with concern at the direction Kuşien went. I, too, was worried about her, but I know she occasionally needed some time alone. As the night wore on, songs and dances weaved stories of old. It was an odd but comforting thought, knowing how such moments could still exist even amidst a turbulent world. Even if I was not racially an Anglo-Elf, I was one culturally and noticed some similarities in the millennia-old stories told by the Mustalf. It caught my attention that some of their tragic stories mentioned unions between them and different races, and that the children of such unions were always born Mustalf. This was the opposite for elves, whose offspring with humans were always born with a more human appearance, no matter how many generations of 'cleansing' with more elven blood occurred. Still, in both cultures the theme of sorrowfully outliving their non-elven partners was prevalent. I pretended not to notice Elna staring at me. During one such story, she approached me. "My mother was actually a human... It's not that uncommon for us to harbour other races, especially if they're useful." "I see." I replied briefly, noticing the lack of non-Mustalf in the caravan despite the new information. "Do you remember when Elder Yarkeva suggested that you should stay? We have no light mages in this caravan, and I think I..." We each felt a hand grabbing our shoulders from behind. It was Tethys, gracefully interrupting Elna once more. "Come on now, little one. If you linger too long, she's bound to tell you her true name." Elna said something in the Mustalf language, clearly irritated judging by her expression. Tethys replied in Anglo-Elven so that I could understand. "Have you not learnt anything from your father's situation? I'm not saying you should only go for other Mustalf, but I know your emotions can be a tad... intense, let's say. Our human friend here clearly has a mission. Don't make things harder for him." After that, Elna seemed more withdrawn. Other women joined her, speaking in hushed tones about things I could only wonder. As the night went on and people left the fire for their tents, I felt weary and decided to head for the small tent they had prepared for me. Kunnebudo approached me, nudging my arm. "Quite cute that kunneauhe, isn't she? Is anything going to happen?" 'Kunne' meant 'dark, black' and 'auhe' was a transliteration of 'elf', the composite word clearly meaning 'Dark Elf'. "I wouldn't say so." She grinned, her prominent canines glinting under the moonlight. "We Keiozhazrun have a proverb. 'Yakosa amya nehurtuma airgakor sime'. You're not lonely, are you?" (the saying meant literally 'Loneliness can become a shining fang') I shook my head. "Not as long as I'm with your group." She chuckled and left, wishing me a good night. Later, for the first time in a few days, I slept without having visions or nightmares.
The next morning, we gathered our belongings, saying our farewells to our gracious hosts. The memory of the night’s joy contrasted with the tension that now settled over us. As I prepared to leave, I felt a gentle tug on my sleeve. It was Elna, her golden eyes looking at me with a mix of hope and sorrow. “Please, Caelan...” she began, her voice soft yet pleading. “Stay with us. Your journey might be perilous, and I can’t bear the thought of you being in danger.” I took a deep breath. “My path will be long and winding.” I replied, my tone gentle but firm. “Our lifespans are too different. You know that.” She looked down, her shoulders slumping with resignation. “I know. But… I can’t help it.” I placed a hand on her shoulder, giving her a reassuring squeeze. “I don’t even know if I’ll see this caravan again, or if I’ll make it alive. It’s better to let your feelings go, Elna.” She nodded, understanding the truth of my words. “I will wait for you.” she said quietly, her voice trembling. I shook my head, glancing back at my companions who were waiting for me. Kuşien had her back turned to us, her disposition impatient. “Don’t wait. Live your long life to the fullest with someone who can walk at the same pace. That’s the best thing you can do.” With a reluctant nod, she let me go, stepping back to join Tethys, who gave me a knowing look. We exchanged a few more farewells, and then we were on our way.
As we resumed our journey, I noticed Kuşien seemed even more distant than usual. She kept to herself, her eyes often focused on the horizon or lost in thought. It was clear that something was troubling her, but every attempt to engage her in conversation was met with brief, curt responses. The terrain grew harsher as we moved further into Hazrun territory. The landscape was rugged, with rocky outcroppings and steep inclines that tested our stamina. Despite the challenging path, we pressed on, driven by Manmurekan’s determination to reach her village. Our progress was halted when we encountered a group of Hazrun bandits. They emerged from behind boulders and trees, their swords drawn, spears and bows prepared, and expressions fierce. The leader, a tall, scarred Hazrun with three horns, stepped forward, his orange eyes narrowing as he looked us over. “Who are you, and what business do you have in these lands?” he demanded, his voice rough and commanding. Before we could respond, the bandit’s gaze landed on Manmurekan’s forehead tattoo. His eyes widened in recognition, and he quickly sheathed his long sword, bowing. “We beg your forgiveness.” he said, using the honorific pronoun 'wohare' instead of the informal 'wome'. “We did not know of your lineage.” Manmurekan stepped forward, her expression calm but authoritative. “We are merely passing through. Thank you for letting us go.” The bandit leader nodded, signalling his men to stand down. “You may pass. Safe travels, three-eyed one.” With that, they stepped aside, allowing us to continue. I felt relieved as we walked away, wondering about Manmurekan’s lineage. When we finally arrived at her village, her joy was palpable. She hurried ahead calling out names and was soon greeted by a group of women; her sisters, mother, and grandmother. They all bore the same forehead tattoo as Manmurekan, marking them as part of the same clan. They embraced her warmly, their voices filled with excitement and love. However, their expressions shifted when they noticed me. They spoke quietly, questioning Manmurekan about my presence. Though I could understand part of what they were saying despite their different Hazrunic dialect, I pretended to be oblivious, allowing Manmurekan to handle the situation.
“Why have you brought a hornless one to our village?” one of the women asked. Manmurekan’s response was firm: “He is a respected companion. Do not judge him for his lack of horns. There is more to him than you can see.” They exchanged uncertain glances but refrained from further questioning. This, I thought, must be a prejudice among the Hazrun, similar to how the Anglo-Elves viewed humans without elven blood. As we spent time in the village, Taokar expressed his relief at being among his kind again. We spent two or three days resting, preparing for the next leg of our mission.
As we explored the village proper, I took in the surroundings. The village was nestled in a lush valley surrounded by towering, craggy mountains. It had tall trees shielding the area and narrow streams cascading down from the peaks. The homes were constructed from stone and wood, blending seamlessly into the natural landscape. Cleverly engineered terraces (planted with what I assumed was rice) were dotted with small gardens that efficiently utilised the surrounding rugged terrain. The village square was modest and quiet, with a provincial air about it. Children played near the central fountain, their laughter echoing as elders chatted while sitting on stone benches. The place had an air of tranquility that was starkly contrasted against the turmoil and unrest we had known since beginning our journey. Manmurekan led us past various decorated huts, stopping occasionally to introduce us to friends and extended family members who rarely looked at me with no suspicion. We were then led to Manmurekan’s clan home, an impressive structure slightly elevated on a hill. As we entered, the scent of herbs and spices filled the air, mingling with the earthy smell of stone and wood. The walls were lined with shelves filled with items and amulets whose purposes were unknown to me. 
A large, intricately carved wooden table dominated the central room. It was soon filled with various dishes. The family insisted we sit and partake in the meal, their warmth and contrasting with our earlier tension. Manmurekan’s grandmother, a wise and aged woman with a singular horn on her scalp and her silver hair neatly tied, looked at us thoughtfully. “Our Manmurekan has always sought new horizons.” she said, her voice soft but strong. “From a young age, she showed promise and wisdom beyond her years.” Manmurekan, clearly embarrassed by the attention, tried to deflect the praise. Her mother continued. “She went beyond our village to seek knowledge and strength to understand the world beyond these mountains. Once Lady Huzur announced her cultural interchange programme, Manmurekan was the first to volunteer.” Her grandmother spook up once more. "Our clan is numerous. We allowed her to relinquish her duty as a Cintsurun so that she could pursue her interests." She turned towards her granddaughter and continued. "Well, it's not like we could keep her here forever." The word 'Cintsurun' meant some priestly duty, I assumed, since 'cin' means deity, 'tsu' is the possessive particle, and 'run' is person.
After the meal, we ventured out into the night, exploring the village further. Each corner seemed to tell a story, from the elder’s council chamber to the training grounds where the men practiced both armed and unarmed fighting. Manmurekan took us to a secluded spot where a stone altar stood beneath a large, ancient tree with twisting branches. “This is the altar of the 32nd child of Owuşiencin, the Sun Goddess, and Rekancin, the Wind God.” she explained. “A guardian deity who watches over our village. My ancestors made a pact with him and his earthly descendants. Most women of my clan can enter a trance and see beyond the veil of the material world, though I was never too good at it.” It was near this altar that Manmurekan shared more of her personal journey with us. She spoke of her youth, of training under the harsh guidance of clan elders, and of her pursuit of magic knowledge. “I wanted to be more than what my clan tradition had for me. To seek knowledge and bridge understanding with other lands.” she said, her voice filled with conviction. "And we're thankful you left this village." Kuşien said in appreciation. Taokar and Kunnebudo nodded solemnly. I observed their smiles as they reminisced about their past together. 
We spent another day in the village, simply resting and preparing for the next stretch of our journey. Manmurekan left us during that period to spend time with her family. The next morning, as dawn crept over the mountains, it was time to leave. Manmurekan stood with her family one last time, her eyes glistening with unshed tears. Her mother pulled her into a tight embrace, whispering words of encouragement and love, repeatedly reassuring her they would be well. Manmurekan reluctantly let go, her resolve steeling as she turned to us. “I am ready,” she said. "It's good to know the war hasn't yet reached the mountains." While we still had the momentum of our departure, we continued our journey. Our path took us through rugged terrain, which we traversed with difficulty until we left the mountains. Time passed quickly, and before we knew it, the sun dipped below the horizon, bathing the landscape in dusk. As night approached, we stumbled upon an abandoned village. Its silent, decayed houses casting long shadows that seemed to reach for us in the diminishing light. After scanning the area and concluding that it was safe, we decided to make camp there for the night.
Then came the division of tasks. Kunnebudo and I were assigned the job of finding wood. Taokar sought a reliable water source while Manmurekan would handle lighting the fire once we returned, and lastly, Kuşien would search for anything edible. Manmurekan gave me a quick lesson in fire magic, creating a small ball of flame that floated close to her. It seemed so effortless. “Focus on keeping it alight and close.” she explained. “Infuse it with just enough mana to sustain itself.” I emulated her spell, replicating her hand seals, replacing the ones corresponding to 'fire' with 'light' and trying to focus my light magic in the same way. A small luminous sphere appeared before me, but unlike Manmurekan’s flame, it was stationary. “It doesn’t move.” I said, a bit disheartened. Manmurekan’s red eyes examined the light sphere. “It’s still useful. Cast some of these around the house we’ll use.” Nodding, I did as instructed, placing magical orbs of light in strategic positions to illuminate our makeshift camp. Taokar returned with disappointing news. “The well is filled with mud.” he said with a grim face, giving up on finding drinkable water nearby. With this, I headed out to find wood, Kunnebudo having already left before me. I explored the deserted houses, collecting broken pieces of furniture. My eyes wandered over parts of the village, noticing signs of fire damage but seeing no skeletons or remains. I couldn’t help but wonder how long it had been since this settlement was last inhabited.
Returning with my arms full of broken furniture, I piled it inside the house’s central fire pit, where Kunnebudo’s pile already laid. Inside, Manmurekan and Kunnebudo had been busy, making the place more livable by clearing debris and arranging a rudimentary seating area. Taokar stood outside, scouting for any potential threats. I helped them tidy up the place further until it actually looked like a reasonable shelter. Soon after, Kuşien returned with a small bag in hand, her expression indicating that her foraging had not yielded much. “Kujanermocaro, reinajorbun, a couple of kwaroai, and some small roots. I found nothing else,” she reported. My eyebrows shot up. “We’re really going to eat that?” I said as I saw the bag filled with crickets, snails, and two frogs. Kuşien’s return look was almost challenging. “Are you saying you won’t?” I shrugged, trying not to show my apprehension. The animal names, I rationalised, were almost intuitive. 'Ku-janer-mocaro' meant 'small-jumping-bug', and 'Rein-ajor-bun' meant 'armour-slithering-thing'. They explained to me that 'Kwaro' was the noise the frogs made, thus 'Kwaroai' meant 'croaker'. Manmurekan lit the fire with a quick spell, the flames dancing and casting warm light around the abandoned home. Taokar found some more resistant wood and quickly shaped it into skewers, piercing the ingredients and setting them by the fire to cook. I watched, partly fascinated and partly dreading.
Once everything was ready, they handed me a skewer first. They were looking at me expectantly. I took a deep breath and bit into a frog leg, which to my surprise, tasted quite good. However, the cricket and the snail were unpalatable. “The frog was tasty, but I can’t say the same for the cricket and snail. The tuber could need some seasoning.” Taokar took a hearty bite himself and nodded. “Crickets are better when fried.” Bemused by their culinary, I found myself joining in despite my initial reluctance. The sense of camaraderie dispelled any lingering concerns, and we all began to eat our strange meal, their casual chatter making the unusual supper feel less oppressive. After dinner a whole day of walking's exertion caught up to me. I settled in, the fire’s warmth and the effect of my spells scattering a comforting glow throughout the house. Once again, I slept soundly. No visions haunted me in my sleep, it was a welcome dreamless night. This, however, made me dread the next visions that were yet to come. The next day, just as the sun rose, I left for a secluded spot behind one of the houses on the outskirts to attend to nature's call. I looked all around me and, after reassuring myself I was alone, I let the impurities from my body flow away, so to speak. Just before I was about to finish, I heard a hum, immediately interrupting the 'stream'. It came not from the left, the right, or from behind me, but from above. As I hurriedly fastened my trousers, I looked up to see Kunnebudo’s golden eyes looking at me. It looked as if she was lying on the roof of the house. "Worry not." She said as she gracefully jumped down. "I won't bite." "How long were you looking?" I asked, feeling a mix of outrage and shame. "Just enough. That's not why I sought you, however." She approached slowly. "I needed you apart from the others because we need to talk about something." There was no way I could defend myself. In virtue of her speed and precision, I'd wager Kunnebudo was the deadliest of the group. I didn't feel any bloodlust coming from her. It was as if she was devoid of emotions, a true cold killer that makes her targets oblivious. "A little grey bird told me that..." She started. I felt my heart pounding wildly within my chest. "...You're from Igirith." My eyes widened, and I instinctively reached for the wall behind me. Before I could utter a word, Kunnebudo was already there, her breath brushing against my skin. In a blink, she closed the distance. Her left hand traced my neck with a sharp fingernail, menacingly pinning me against the wall with her right hand near my shoulder. Although she was a petite woman and shorter than me, I had never felt more threatened in my life. "W-who told..." I stammered, halted by her finger on my lips. "A little grey bird in the caravan, I said. But I'm not your enemy, this shall be our... little secret, yes? I won't tell the others." She slowly withdrew, breaking the close contact between us. Panting, I felt my legs tremble. 
"I am not your enemy, Caelan. But who knows how Kuşien and Taokar would react to this information?" She approached again, this time cupping my ears and pulling my face closer to hers, though it didn't seem like she was going for a kiss. Once our foreheads touched, we both felt what I can only describe as an electric shock. My head recoiled backwards, hitting the wall behind me, while Kunnebudo, wincing from the pain, rubbed her forehead to soothe the pain. "Oww... Is that some trickery from that Eye?" "Erm... I don't know... But if you're not my enemy, why are you acting so menacingly?" Kunnebudo looked wide-eyed at me. "Wait... Say that again." It then dawned on me that I had spoken in Anglo-Elven, not in Hazrunic. I repeated the sentence as Kunnebudo scratched her head. "It seems you transferred knowledge to me, I think. Somehow... I mean only knowledge, not memories." She paced back and forth. "What if it went both ways?" Kunnebudo seemed excited. "I'll sing a song that you've never heard and let's see if you can understand it!" 
"Eiz keioz tsu naşa (In this river)
Gyakigere ripuna (Fish swim)
Tera-tera, oterez (Swaying, swaying, [they] went)
Hu tura se mitertsez ([They] showed a blue colour)
Eiz eri setan haka (At this place, I)
Sagwu tsuri tsu cenar (Wait during the rain)
Tera, nugata, akate (Swaying, shapeless, until)
Wome aşer coyake" (You come close)
Her singing was a bit different from the Hazrunic I was used to. It gave me the impression she was speaking in a dialect, of which I could understand each word. "It's as if I have spoken Hazrunic my whole life... How strange..." I then translated the lyrics to Anglo-Elven as Kunnebudo bounced in excitement, her cold killer eyes gone in an instant. Truly a spontaneous woman. "We shouldn't mention to the others that you now speak Anglo-Elven. How would we explain it? My origins, I mean." I said. "No worries, we'll just say you did some Eye magic and learnt Hazrunic all of a sudden. You won't be able to mask the Keiozhazrun dialect anyways, they're bound to see through it. As for my knowing of the enemy's language, that's another secret between us."
We returned to the group. Upon hearing the news, they seemed curious. "It's humorous... Now you speak in the same way as Kunnebudo. Even the inflections and tones." Manmurekan mused. I think they already expected the Eye of Ma'at to grant supernatural abilities. She then narrowed her eyes slightly, her curiosity mixed with a cautious undertone. “But it’s a bit too convenient, isn’t it?” she mused aloud. “The Eye of Ma’at suddenly grants you the ability to speak Hazrunic? Just like that?” Kuşien folded her arms, regarding me with a skeptical gaze. “Did anything unusual happen before you could understand us?” I exchanged a quick look with Kunnebudo, who nodded subtly, encouraging me to proceed. “Well, Kunnebudo and I… sort of accidentally bumped our foreheads together.” Kunnebudo quickly elaborated, her words spilling out in a hurried explanation. “We didn’t intend for anything strange to happen... It’s a new law passed to help young offenders progress and as part of your rehabilitation, I wanted to send this letter as soon as I could.I know this is the first time you’re hearing of this but we hoped it would benefit you more than doing nothing. We tried to prevent you serving time but there were too many riots. Too many angry people. I’m sorry. I tried.I must keep who I am, anonymous due to the part of the legislation passed; it’s part of the rules but I also think is for the best currently. I can't give you any hints as to who I am apart from telling you that I am your age. I’m meant to be relatable. If you guess, I can’t tell you whether you are right or wrong. Prisoners are matched with those who they can relate too. Your father is unfortunately too old to be able to participate as it’s for under 20 only. He is well. As is your mother. I thought you would like to know that she isn’t allowed to visit you. She’s on house arrest, part of the loosened sentence she got in helping Harry Potter.We didn’t think it was quite fair that you were sentenced to two years in Azkaban but if you comply, we can get the sentence reduced to a year. I know this doesn’t seem like quite the exciting thing for you to do, but I thought it would at least help you to not go insane. I can only imagine the horrors in there and I’m sorry you have to go though it. I hope these help, even if it’s a little.It’s currently September 19th, 1998. The temperature outside is a warm 19 degrees. The wind is slightly cooler and its rather grey, out.These letters will come once every two weeks. It gives you time for your letter in-between.I hope to hear from you soon. Please let me know if you want to know anything, I will see what I can do. I just didn’t want to make your first letter, too long and too overwhelming.Hello and goodbye.:) x'

Korean Teachers' Union Calls for Cancellation of Live-Action Webtoon-Based Get Schooled Series

The Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union (KTU), also known as JeonGyoJo, has publicly opposed the production of the upcoming Netflix series adaptation of the webtoon Get Schooled, calling for its cancellation due to concerns over its portrayal of violence and the education system.



On May 20, the union released a statement titled “Violence Is Not True Education,” urging Netflix and the production team to halt the drama. The union criticized the original webtoon for its "sensational depiction of conflict between students, parents, and teachers" and for portraying educators as "incompetent and passive." It argued that the story glamorizes violence in schools and undermines the professional dignity and expertise of teachers.



“The issue with adapting Get Schooled into a drama is that it legitimizes violence by portraying a government-backed character who assaults students under the pretext of protecting teachers' rights,” the union stated. “This not only weakens trust in democratic conflict resolution within schools but also distorts efforts to build a human rights-friendly education environment and restore public education.”



KTU further emphasized that "violence is not true education" and that infringing on students' rights under the guise of teacher protection is unacceptable. While acknowledging the importance of creative freedom, the union stressed that content creators should consider their social responsibility and influence.



Get Schooled, which has been serialized on Naver Webtoon since November 2020, tells the story of Hwa-jin Na, an officer from the Ministry of Education's Teacher Protection Bureau, who takes matters into his own hands to restore order in schools following the passage of a law banning corporal punishment. The series explores the challenges of maintaining authority in schools and delivering justice.



While the original webtoon gained attention for its satisfying narratives driven by strong state power, it also drew criticism for portraying marginalized groups such as women and people of color as villains, often resolving conflict through violence.



Jong-chan Hong (Juvenile Justice, Mr. Plankton) is directing the series, and Nam-kyu Lee (Behind Your Touch, The Light in Your Eyes) is writing. Director Hong has acknowledged the above concerns and previously stated that the drama adaptation will approach the material with greater sensitivity and care.



Get Schooled is written by Yong-taek Chae and drawn by Ga-ram Han.



Ablaze Publishing is releasing the series in print. WEBTOON Entertainment previously released part the series in English digitally, but has since removed the title from its service.

He picked up the sheaf of papers off the table and ruffled through them rapidly. "There is no precedent," he added. "I had hoped," said Andrew Young, "to establish precedent." Commissioner Stanford said, "I must admit that you have made a good case, Ancestor Young. Yet you must realize that this commission has no possible jurisdiction over the life of any person, except to see that everyone is assured of all the benefits of immortality and to work out any kinks that may show up." "I am well aware of that," answered Young, "and it seems to me that my case is one of the kinks you mention." He stood silently, watching the faces of the members of the board. They are afraid, he thought. Every one of them. Afraid of the day they will face the thing I am facing now. They have sought an answer and there is no answer yet except the pitifully basic answer, the brutally fundamental answer that I have given them. "My request is simple," he told them, calmly. "I have asked for permission to discontinue life. And since suicide has been made psychologically impossible, I have asked that this commission appoint a panel of next-friends to make the necessary and somewhat distasteful arrangements to bring about the discontinuance of my life." "If we did," said Riggs, "we would destroy everything we have. There is no virtue in a life of only five thousand years. No more than in a life of only a hundred years. If Man is to be immortal, he must be genuinely immortal. He cannot compromise." "And yet," said Young, "my friends are gone." He gestured at the papers Riggs held in his hands. "I have them listed there," he said. "Their names and when and where and how they died. Take a look at them. More than two hundred names. People of my own generation and of the generations closely following mine. Their names and the photo-copies of their death certificates." He put both of his hands upon the table, palms flat against the table, and leaned his weight upon his arms. "Take a look at how they died," he said. "Every one involves accidental violence. Some of them drove their vehicles too fast and, more than likely, very recklessly. One fell off a cliff when he reached down to pick a flower that was growing on its edge. A case of deliberately poor judgment, to my mind. One got stinking drunk and took a bath and passed out in the tub. He drowned...." "Ancestor Young," Riggs said sharply, "you are surely not implying these folks were suicides." "No," Andrew Young said bitterly. "We abolished suicide three thousand years ago, cleared it clean out of human minds. How could they have killed themselves?" Stanford said, peering up at Young, "I believe, sir, you sat on the board that resolved that problem." Andrew Young nodded. "It was after the first wave of suicides. I remember it quite well. It took years of work. We had to change human perspective, shift certain facets of human nature. We had to condition human reasoning by education and propaganda and instill a new set of moral values. I think we did a good job of it. Perhaps too good a job. Today a man can no more think of deliberately committing suicide than he could think of overthrowing our government. The very idea, the very word is repulsive, instinctively repulsive. You can come a long way, gentlemen, in three thousand years." He leaned across the table and tapped the sheaf of papers with a lean, tense finger. "They didn't kill themselves," he said. "They did not commit suicide. They just didn't give a damn. Boards, commissions, legislative posts, diplomatic missions. No one can say that I have shirked my duty. I submit that I have paid any debt I owe humanity ... even the well-intentioned debt for a chance at immortality." "We wish," said Riggs, "that you would reconsider." "I am a lonely man," replied Young. "A lonely man and tired. I have no friends. There is nothing any longer that holds my interest. It was one of the problems which was recognized when immortality first became practical. But we always thought that memory would erase itself, that the brain could accommodate only so many memories, that when it got full up it would dump the old ones. It hasn't worked that way." He made a savage gesture. "Gentlemen, I can recall my childhood much more vividly than I recall anything that happened yesterday." "Memories are buried," said Riggs, "and in the old days, when men lived no longer than a hundred years at most, it was thought those buried memories were forgotten. A man's desires are few, and quickly sated, and yet he is expected to continue living with desires burned up and blown away to ash. Remembered it as clearly as if it had been a thing that had happened in the morning of this very day. It was a shining thing, a bright thing, a happiness that was brand-new and fresh as a bluebird's wing of an April morning or a shy woods flower after sudden rain. He had been a boy and he had seen the bluebird and he had no words to say the thing he felt, but he had held up his tiny fingers and pointed and shaped his lips to coo. Once, he thought, I had it in my very fingers and I did not have the experience to know what it was, nor the value of it. And now I know the value, but it has escaped me--it escaped me on the day that I began to think like a human being. The first adult thought pushed it just a little and the next one pushed it farther and finally it was gone entirely and I didn't even know that it had gone. 꽤 넓은 사무실로 다른 외국인이 입장했다. 민머리 남자. 퍽 익숙한 얼굴. 조셉의 오른팔 격인 부하 직원인 로버트였다. 그를 보자마자 조셉이 바로 물었다.



“로버트, 넘긴 일은 잘 처리했나?”



“예. 스탭들에게 잘 전달했습니다. 그보다 조셉.”



퍽 진지한 얼굴인 로버트가 앉은 조셉에게 붙어 약간 목소리를 죽였다.



“‘컬럼비아 스튜디오’ 쪽 재밌는 소문이 돕니다.”



“아- ‘컬럼비아 스튜디오’? 새 영화 제작 건으로 안 그래도 시끄럽던데. 안가복 감독을 기용한 것도 신선했고. 무슨 소문이지?”



“와전된 것 같긴 한데, 크리스 하트넷이 ‘컬럼비아 스튜디오’ 본사 앞에서 아시아 배우와 신경전을 벌였답니다.”



태블릿을 내려보던 조셉이 미간을 좁히면서도 고개를 들었다.



“음? 크리스가? 성격이 좀 확고한 편이긴 해도 그 친구가 괜한 분란을 만드는 편이 아닌데- 확실히 좀 와전된 거 같군.”



“적당한 말다툼이 오갔고, 그 아시아 배우가 크리스의 이름을 물었다고 합니다.”



“하하, 재밌네. 크리스의 이름을 물었어? 그건 의도한 거야. 크리스가 한 방 제대로 먹은 셈이네. 근데 크리스가 이 타이밍에 ‘컬럼비아 스튜디오’에 갔다라- 안가복 감독이 맡은 작품의 남주 후보로 올랐나?”



“아무래도.”



“정보를 업데이트해야겠어. 그나저나 소문이 진짜면 그 아시아 배우는 꽤 센데? 헐리웃에서, 그것도 ‘컬럼비아 스튜디오’ 앞마당에서 그런 사건을 당당히 벌였다는 거잖아? 어디 배우야? 중국?”



고개를 저은 로버트의 목소리가 더 줄었다.



“아무래도 강우진 같습니다.”



순간, 움직임을 멈춘 조셉의 눈이 디립다 커졌고.



“어?”



벌떡 일어나 강하게 되물었다.



“뭐? 강우진??!”



소문이 생각보다 가팔랐다.

Ellie the Explorer:
Ellie is a charismatic and adventurous young woman with a passion for exploring the cosmos. She has short, spiky hair dyed a vibrant shade of purple, and her eyes are an enchanting shade of green, sparkling with curiosity and determination. She wears a sleek, retro-futuristic space jacket with a colorful array of patches from different planets she's visited. Her outfit includes sturdy boots and a utility belt filled with gadgets for her interstellar escapades. Ellie's enthusiasm is infectious, and her leadership keeps the team united through any challenge.

Dr. Wyatt the Skeptic Scientist:
Dr. Wyatt is meticulous and keen-minded, with a penchant for questioning the unexplained. He sports a pair of round spectacles that occasionally slide down his nose when he's deep in thought. His hair is neatly combed, its color a dusty shade of gray, adding a distinguished look to his youthful face. Dressed in a simple white lab coat over a navy-blue turtleneck, he always carries a small tablet device for notes and observations. Though skeptical, Dr. Wyatt approaches the wonders of the galaxy with an open mind, ever seeking evidence to expand his understanding.

Fluff, the Rabbit-Shaped Slime Creature:
Fluff is an adorable, gelatinous creature resembling a bunny, with ears that wiggle expressively. His body is a translucent shade of light blue, with a soft sheen that shimmers in the light. Fluff's eyes are large and animated, filled with sparkle and wonder, reflecting his playful personality. Although amorphous, he often maintains his rabbit-like shape to bounce around with an irresistible cuteness. Fluff's ability to change forms makes him a lively and handy companion on their adventures.

Flo, the Sister of Fluff:
Flo, like her brother Fluff, is a slime creature who takes the form of a rabbit, but her color is a soft pastel pink with a glistening glow. Her ears are slightly longer than Fluff’s, and she often uses them to convey her thoughts through gesture. Flo’s demeanor is gentle and nurturing, providing a calming balance to Fluff’s exuberance. Despite her amorphous nature, she can change into various shapes when needed, contributing her creativity and grace to the team's endeavors.

King Celestial, the Fallen Monarch:
King Celestial is a regally poised figure who once ruled a mighty star kingdom. He wears a tattered robe adorned with cosmic symbols and a crooked crown that hints at his former grandeur. His skin has an ethereal glow, resembling stardust scattered across the night sky, with hair resembling a silver comet's trail. His eyes, deep and wise, hold the secrets of countless galaxies. Despite his fallen status, King Celestial carries himself with dignity and seeks redemption and understanding of the universe beyond his lost kingdom.

Together, these distinct characters blend their unique appearances and personalities to embark on thrilling adventures through the galaxy, learning from each other and the cosmos along the way. This picturesque world is a realm where the landscape seems almost alive, constantly shifting and shimmering with an otherworldly beauty.

Geography and Environment:

Gelatopia's surface is a mesmerizing mosaic of gently rolling hills, crystal-clear lakes, and lush, gelatinous forests. The terrain is soft, almost bouncy, creating a whimsical sensation for anyone traversing it. The trees and plants resemble delicate sculptures made of translucent jelly, their colors changing with the shifting light of the two suns that illuminate the planet. When the wind blows, the flora gently sways, producing a melodic hum that fills the air, adding an auditory layer to the planet's charm.

The climate of Gelatopia is consistently mild and pleasant, with a perfect balance of warmth and cool breezes. Put in your claim before it's too late! This is an excerpt from a story that appeared on the BBC this past August (2007). The text below the map explains the numbers.

"The Russians are leading a new 'gold rush' in the high north, with a bold attempt to assert a claim to oil, gas and mineral rights over large parts of the Arctic Ocean up to the North Pole."

1) North Pole: Russia leaves its flag on the seabed, 4,000m (13,100ft) beneath the surface, as part of its claims for oil and gas reserves2) Lomonosov Ridge: Russia argues that this underwater feature is an extension of its continental territory and is looking for evidence3) 200-nautical mile (370km) line: Shows how far countries' agreed economic area extends beyond their coastline. Often set from outlying islands4) Russian-claimed territory: The bid to claim a vast area is being closely watched by other countries. Some could follow suit

Some interesting solutions that appear in this story:

The "median line method", supported by Canada and Denmark, would divide the Arctic waters between countries according to their length of nearest coastline. This would give Denmark the Pole itself but Canada would gain as well.

The "sector method" would take the North Pole as the centre and draw lines south along longitudes. This would penalise Canada but Norway and, to a lesser extent, Russia, would gain.

The Map of Mexico 1550 Project was designed by Lily Diaz, a professor at Media Lab Helsinki. The map is reputed to have been authored by Alonso de Santa Cruz, royal cosmographer to emperor Charles V of Spain. It resides at the Uppsala University Library in Sweden. She took a series of overlapping, stereo images of the map and pieced them together as one digital image. Then a series of historical points of interest were laid on top with descriptions, photos and web links. As you zoom in on regions of the map these squares will get larger and pop up information as you hover over them. The author's description of the map is below:

"Painted on two sheets of parchment joined together at the center, the map shows the city surrounded by water and with canals between its buildings. The familial sporadic classification: its power for the resolution of genetic and environmental etiologic factors.
An increasingly popular research method for identifying etiologic heterogeneity in psychiatric illness has been to compare the frequency of a risk factor in affected individuals with no affected relatives (sporadic cases) and in affected individuals with one or more affected relatives (familial cases). This paper presents a power analysis of this familial vs sporadic method, assuming a multifactorial model with a normally distributed liability to illness resulting from the additive effect of polygenes and multiple environmental factors. Various parameter estimates for a risk factor that identifies a component of either the genetic or the environmental contribution to disease liability are examined. Almost without exception, large sample sizes of probands and relatives need to be studied to have a substantial probability of detecting etiologic heterogeneity. The required sample size decreases dramatically when monozygotic twins are studied. If the multifactorial model accurately depicts the etiology for psychiatric disorders, these results suggest that the familial versus sporadic design is useful only when pursued in the context of large sample nuclear family studies or studies of monozygotic twins.
